title: The Midterm Conventions Will Continue Until Morale Improves
excerpt: If only the GOP midterm convention succeeds in its aim of electing Donald Trump president, things will get a lot better in this country
body: If only the GOP midterm convention succeeds in its aim of electing Donald Trump president, things will get a lot better in this country

Isn’t he already president? Hush! At the Unprecedented (But Very President-ed) Republican Midterm Convention, we reject such trivial objections! “I know many of you are still struggling thanks to Joe Biden and the Democrats,” said Richard Hudson, the National Republican Committee chair

You have your orders: Imagine that Donald Trump is on the ballot , because if he were, the economy would get a lot better than it is under whoever is president right now—I have to assume Biden? But possibly, based on sheer volume of mentions, Abdul El-Sayed? Whoever it is, the guy is doing just terribly
Donald Trump has already fixed everything, but also, we need him to fix everything
He is the greatest president in our lifetime, if we can ever manage to elect him
Also, everything is on the verge of being taken from us by Democrats
Communists! “Communism is on the march, and it’s up to us to stop it in its tracks!” announced Donald Trump Jr. (whom the C-SPAN chyron demurely introduces as a 1789 Capital partner)

Communists, he said, are “triggered at the sight of an American flag” and want to turn our cities into a “dystopian hellscape.” “Democrats are advocates for evil,” warned the pastor introducing the second day of festivities

Senator Ted Cruz denounced the “red-green alliance” of “Communists and Islamists”: “They hate Christians, they hate Jews, they hate capitalism, they hate the Constitution, and they hate America.” Things remained at this feverish pitch of Two Minutes’ Hate (sadly not limited to two minutes) for most of the convention

There were hearty scoops of anti-immigrant sentiment, Islamophobia (most speakers tackled El-Sayed’s name as though even attempting to pronounce it aloud was an unreasonable demand), and fearmongering about “TRANSGENDER FOR EVERYONE!” (as the president put it)
It’s wonderful that things are going so well that we can take a step back and focus on what really matters: making this country a worse place for people to live in

Vance stepped onstage on the second night and complained that “we were tired of being called racists for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer and less safe and less prosperous.” Can’t imagine why anyone would suggest that there were racist implications in a statement like that! He had some equally un-grotesque remarks to offer about James Talarico’s support for trans kids (“I never want to see that guy’s web-browser history”)

Vance—more and more lifelike every day—got the warmest welcome he could possibly have wanted, often pausing his speech to bask in the applause, and even attempting to tell the women behind him that they looked good (“If you’re ever feeling down about our country,” he said, “just take a look at the beautiful ladies right behind me”) and to say that if they were having beverages, he wanted some too

Some people even chanted “48!,” which left him starry-eyed. (“I got to say, it’s pretty cool to hear a crowd that’s this fired up chant your name.”) Said fired-up crowd was a sore subject that the president harped on in both of his speeches, urging people not to go to the bathroom lest someone snap a photo of their empty seat and draw incorrect conclusions
After Vance’s speech, the night took an even more surreal turn
Trump returned to the stage and promised that he would not repeat the speech from the previous night
Then he began to repeat the speech from the previous night
As the desiccated corpse of the previous speech came shambling back to finish its unfinished business, I began to worry that we were all trapped in some kind of time loop
How to break it? Vote Trump? More tenor? Whatever beverage the beautiful women were having? “It was bad, but now it’s good

And it’s going to soon be greater than ever before.” (This is what I, too, would say if I were trying to remember the general gist of the president’s Wednesday-night remarks but had no access to a teleprompter.) For a second night in a row, the president warned about the “mutilization” of children

He also repeated his promise of a $5,000 “let’s call it Trump dividend” for all Americans if they vote Republican majorities into both houses of Congress. (Is this legal?) This money would be for adults, Trump clarified: “We love our adults
It’s time we take care of our adults.” Yes! Those freeloading, nonvoting children have rested their tiny booties on our necks too long
Then he forced everyone to listen to his “presidential tenor,” Chris Macchio, sing “ Nessun dorma ” as balloons fell
Also “All I Ask of You” from The Phantom of the Opera
No one makes anything up anymore, except the AI you are asking for urgent medical advice

At one point during this ramble, after making everyone raise one hand and swear to bring their family to the polls (and cheat, if necessary), the president told everyone that if they did not vote, they would go to hell

title: The AI Pandemic Isn’t On Its Way
excerpt: Last month, a team of scientists published a high-profile paper describing how they’d taught an AI model to help produce brand-new, deadly viruses
body: Last month, a team of scientists published a high-profile paper describing how they’d taught an AI model to help produce brand-new, deadly viruses
The AI—a “genome-language model” trained on DNA sequences—had designed multiple new genomes that scientists then synthesized into functional viruses
And some of those viruses were capable of killing bacteria in a dish
The loudest reaction to the study (which had been released as a preprint about a year ago) was fear
Now that AI can design viruses that go after bacteria, perhaps someone could use the technology to manufacture pathogens that harm people—sparking a major outbreak, even a devastating pandemic
This potential threat evoked some of the same concerns that politicians , researchers , and tech leaders (including Bill Gates ) have raised

And these fears are only gaining traction: On Thursday, Anthropic released a report that sparked a round of doom-laden headlines, detailing several instances in which the company banned accounts that were using its LLM, Claude, for what could have been reputable research efforts—or efforts to develop biological weapons

AI, which has repeatedly proved itself capable of exceeding user expectations and bypassing guardrails, is a formidable force; many fears about its potential biological threat stem from its relentless pace of development and the possibility that it could make independent breakthroughs, exceeding researchers’ own understanding, especially if AIs eventually achieve recursive self-improvement—that is, models designing newer and smarter models

Kevin Esvelt, a biologist at MIT and a co-founder of Secure Bio, a biosecurity nonprofit, told me that although he thinks the probability of an AI-driven pandemic remains quite low, the consequences of such a catastrophe would be so large that “it’s very important that we drive that probability down as low as we can.” But many other biologists, especially infectious-disease experts and virologists, told me that the threat of a pandemic need not loom particularly large on the list of AI-made threats

To the scientists most familiar with the minutiae of growing, modifying, and testing viruses in a lab, and the havoc they can wreak in the real world, the viruses that have already arisen through evolution, or will soon enough, still present much more immediate perils
In other words, humans should be investing aggressively in pandemic preparation, but not because of AI
To be clear, viruses made with the help of AI could pose some threat
The experts I spoke with agreed that, in the wrong hands, AI could be used to speed infectious destruction, to a degree
To create the bacterium-killing virus, scientists led by a group at Stanford University and the Arc Institute fed the AI model, called Evo, only viral genomes that attack bacteria
Those genomes are much simpler and smaller than ones coding for viruses that go after humans
In theory, though, with a similar technique, researchers could train AI on the genomes of viruses that infect humans, with the aim of manufacturing novel pathogens

Or perhaps—as some people worry is likelier, easier, and more dangerous—users could ask AI to adjust specific traits of viruses known to cause disease, until those pathogens can skirt available vaccines
Scientists have long been able to manipulate viral genetics without AI

This kind of “gain of function” research has stirred its own political and scientific controversy—especially in discussions about the origins of COVID-19 —and the Trump administration has restricted federal funding for it

But current AI models have the capacity to “put a supreme battery in the back of the things that people were already doing,” Brandon Ogbunu, an evolutionary biologist and infectious-diseases modeler at Yale University, told me
Tom Inglesby, the director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, worries about bad actors using AI to surmount some of the limits of their own technical expertise

Ideally, models powerful enough to suggest new viral genomes should be subject to strict, formal review, Inglesby said; perhaps they could even be limited to training on only certain types of benign data. (For instance, the team that built Evo trained it only on viruses that kill bacteria, and withheld any data about viruses that can harm more complex life forms, including humans.) Esvelt advocates for restricting access to certain models entirely

Other researchers, however, including the virologists I spoke with, pointed out that another set of safeguards is already in place: how little we humans—the creators and users of AI—understand about pathogenic viruses
For AI to map out more effective pathogens, people must be able to feed it data on what makes viruses highly transmissible, dangerous, and able to circumvent immune safeguards

But these concepts are complex and murky enough that the chasm AI would need to cross is wide; researchers lack much of the basic knowledge they’d need to train an AI properly on such topics. “Right now, the data is junk going in,” Seema Lakdawala, a virologist at Emory University, told me

Generations of virologists have not come up with firm answers to key questions about what makes certain viruses better at causing diseases than others, or why some people are more susceptible to particular infections than others
Even expert virologists may struggle to ask AI the best prompts to guide it in useful directions

In her own research on viral transmission, Lakdawala hasn’t found LLMs such as Claude and ChatGPT particularly helpful or correct, she told me, even when she’s asked it questions far simpler than “How do I make a pandemic virus?” (for example, basic questions about the flu-virus genome)

Brian Hie, the lead researcher on the team that designed Evo, told me he’s also unconvinced “that AI would even be the method of choice for someone trying to make a dangerous pathogen.” It does not know enough about pathogens, because we don’t know enough about pathogens
Esvelt, at MIT, argues that AI might not need to understand viruses perfectly, or even that well, to stumble across a dangerous iteration of one
AIs might also improve rapidly enough to make more sense of the existing data than human researchers ever have
But no matter how good AIs get, they so far have no way to build and test new pathogens, Gigi Gronvall, a health-security expert at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told me

Even a very motivated human—whether they wanted to spark a pandemic for a government or terrorist organization, or for their own ends—would still have to pick through AI-generated possibilities, successfully synthesize them, assess them for enhanced (or at least sufficient) transmissibility and virulence, produce a sufficient quantity to do serious damage, and then release that payload of new virus into the world
All of that requires substantial skill in the lab, as well as expensive equipment and lab animals
It’s not impossible, but it certainly isn’t easy, either

The practice of building new viruses in a laboratory is fickle: “Even if I give two experienced scientists the same protocol, they’re going to do it differently, and the results could come out differently,” Linsey Marr, a viral-transmission researcher at Virginia Tech, told me
Tinkering with viruses the old-fashioned way has also taught researchers that many hypotheses about what should make a virus more contagious or dangerous don’t pan out

Researchers cannot simply tune up a virus’s transmissibility or virulence like a dial; such changes can come with serious costs, including rendering the entire pathogen nonfunctional—incapable of infecting or hurting a person at all
Evolution is already a master at tinkering with life forms and building upon their most successful—or dangerous—traits
Viruses are constantly trying out new versions of themselves and aren’t limited by human expectations about what “dangerous” agents of disease look like

title: AI Writing Has Entered Its Post-Shame Era
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube AI-infused writing is suddenly everywhere: not just in automated email responses or meeting summaries, but in
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube AI-infused writing is suddenly everywhere: not just in automated email responses or meeting summaries, but in books and even the pages of mainstream newspapers
When an editor at The Wall Street Journal recently defended an op-ed that was 100 percent written by AI, it felt like a possible turning point, at which people are no longer apologizing

So is AI-assisted writing in its post-shame era? What does that mean for the way we process, communicate, and think? Host Charlie Warzel talks to the journalists Elizabeth Spiers and Teddy Brown about being a writer when the robots are coming for you, and how technology does not have to be inevitable
The following is a transcript of the episode: Elizabeth Spiers: I just worry that AI is making everybody dumber

I think when you outsource the fundamental cognitive arsenal that you’re using to actually construct a good argument or to make a piece of art, what happens to us as a society if everybody’s outsourcing that to AI models? Teddy Brown: When I worked in tech, I was writing 3,000-page papers about really dense B2B-enterprise marketing strategies, or whatever
And I would get to the end, and it would go onto the website: I have no idea what I wrote about
I could not tell you one thing about that, because it was just all flowing through Claude
Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain , a show where today we’re gonna talk about artificial intelligence and the thing that I do for a living, which is writing
We’re almost four years into the ChatGPT era, and AI writing is everywhere
We’ve got SEO spam, slop—all that synthetic pablum that’s just immediately recognizable
A Pew Research analysis from July estimated that “signs of AI authorship can be found in over one-third of web pages published after ChatGPT was released.” One-third of web pages
It’s come for schools; it’s come for universities, which have been struggling for years to get students to write papers without chatbot assistance
And in professional writing, we’ve watched this slow and steady creep of AI show up in book publishing, in mainstream publications, in op-eds
And for a while, the reaction was all the same

As my colleague Will Oremus wrote recently: “Up to now, those accused of passing off a computer’s writing as their own have tended to either apologize or deny it.” In April, James Taranto, who is The Wall Street Journal ’s editorial features editor, wrote that “those of us who practice writing as a professional craft have an ethical duty and sometimes a contractual obligation to ensure that our work is original.” Now, a few months later, in the same paper, billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller published an op-ed which was identified as 100 percent written by AI
Only this time, there was no deflecting; there was no apologizing
Druckenmiller and the head of The Wall Street Journal’ s opinion pages admitted to and defended the usage of this chatbot to write the op-ed
The head of the opinion page responded: “AI is a fact of modern life.” You hear that a lot now
There’s a lot of people out there who are not professional writers and who don’t want to have to write certain things, like a “just looping back” email to a boss or to a coworker
Last week I had to write an email to a pest-control company about being overcharged for a mousetrap
There’s a lot of writing out there that is drudgery
It is the exact stuff that artificial intelligence automates really, really well
And there’s also the issue here that, as a writer, I may not be the most impartial messenger
Of course, I’m gonna be defensive about this
I don’t want something to come out there and take the one marketable skill that I have and just make it irrelevant
But I also think that there’s something else going on here
Something that goes well beyond what precious writerly types like myself think
Because writing isn’t just a boring, overly formal thing that we have to do to get through school
There’s a lot of debate over whether writing is synonymous with thinking, and well, I’m not sure that it’s one-to-one here
Writing, and especially learning to write effectively, can be a powerful skill that helps advance or sharpen our thinking
Writing is a way to organize our thoughts
It’s a way to set aside quiet, focused time to understand what we really believe about something
It is the scaffolding on which we build arguments, which means that it is, in part, a way to crystallize how we see the world
What I noticed most in the response to this Wall Street Journal op-ed and all the backlash was this group of people arguing that this is where things are going
The toothpaste can’t be put back in the tube, and so we might as well embrace it
It’s a “resistance is futile” type of argument
But the thing about new technologies is that they’re never inevitable

Nor is it written in stone that professional writers and news organizations and people who rely on the trust of their audience to sell a product that is quite literally the craft of written argumentation need to roll over completely without negotiating their own boundaries in this moment
To automate our drudgery is understandable
But to automate such a broad form of communication—to outsource an important tool for working past the roadblocks that exist in our own minds—that’s something different than embracing a new gadget

title: The Spectacle of 1980s Hollywood
excerpt: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
body: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
Jackie Collins, who wrote flashy, sex-filled Hollywood thrillers, isn’t often thought of as a canonical Los Angeles novelist

I didn’t regard her as one, at least—until I read Sophie Gilbert’s essay about Collins , the latest entry in The Atlantic ’s series “ The Writer’s Way .” Collins wrote shiny 1980s “bonkbusters,” as one critic called them; in her novels, including her breakthrough, Hollywood Wives , she turned gossip about scheming producers and backbiting socialites into gripping, soapy dramas long before reality shows made such stories commonplace
Until I learned more about these works, they felt to me like a surface treatment of the complex city best captured by Raymond Chandler, Joan Didion, Octavia Butler, and Eve Babitz
It didn’t help that they were set in Beverly Hills, which, in my nearly five years living in L.A., I knew mostly as a nexus of unaffordable baubles and posh podiatrists’ offices
But Gilbert’s exploration of the writer and the enclave made me realize that her novels fit right into the city’s long literary tradition
First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: The sadness of being the “Last Man” Cereal has strayed too far

The novel that looks death in the eye “ Abstract ,” a poem by Jane Hirshfield In addition to creating steely characters who advanced the idea of middle age as a woman’s powerful prime, Collins was a “devoted” fan of Mickey Spillane, the hardest of hard-boiled-detective novelists, and the influence of noir comes through in her treatment of Beverly Hills: “Jackie genuinely loved the neighborhood for its clean white lines and endless sky,” Gilbert writes, “but she was also drawn to everything it contained beneath the surface: its roiling currents of fame, power, and degradation.” Beneath the shimmering surfaces, dark shadows always lurked. “Sunshine or Noir?” Mike Davis asked in his nonfiction masterpiece about Los Angeles, City of Quartz

The binary of light and dark is ingrained in the L.A. canon; it animates not only Chandler’s literary potboilers, but also Babitz’s sad-girl stories, Butler’s numinous dystopias, and Didion’s alienated meditations

Collins was, like these writers, an insider with an outsider’s soul. “I don’t live the Hollywood lifestyle,” she told an interviewer (while sitting poolside at her stark-white mansion, mind you). “I move in it

I’m an observer.” Gilbert does some observing of her own as she roams Jackie’s neighborhood—she refers to her by first name, like a friend—and she discovers that the city has changed a great deal since Collins’s time

The author captured a different Hollywood, before it was supplanted by “brand-activation opportunities and AI-drafted emails,” before celebrity became “its own art form.” L.A. in the 2020s requires a new kind of best seller, and the city still produces them

This summer in The Atlantic , Carolyn Kellogg wrote about the work of Angeleno Jordan Harper , whose latest novel, A Violent Masterpiece , concerns a TMZ-style celebrity videographer and a plotline ripped from the Epstein files
Steph Cha, Gary Phillips, and Ivy Pochoda “are also bringing today’s Los Angeles, in all its awful, beautiful chaos, to life on the page,” Kellogg notes
Their books don’t repudiate the existence or value of Collins’s 1980s spectacle: They’re proof that L.A. is constantly evolving, and also that it is perennially, insistently itself
Dina Litovsky for The Atlantic Jackie Collins Wrote Her Own Revolution By Sophie Gilbert The novelist imagined women enjoying equality in the bedroom and the boardroom
Are we any closer to living in that world? Read the full article

What to Read Guilty Pleasures , by Arielle Zibrak The smutty hockey romance Heated Rivalry is passionately beloved, yet many of its fans admit to being embarrassed by their obsession with the TV series and novels that inspired it. (Ardent and committed lovers of other things—such as, say, hockey teams—tend not to feel the same way.) But Zibrak, an English professor at the University of Wyoming, insists that no novel, film, or show is more shameful, or less worth consuming, than any other is—and that even art dismissed as lowbrow has “much to tell us about ourselves and the world.” In this short, snappy tract, she confidently surveys the landscape of “guilty pleasures”—usually those written by, about, or for women—and unearths newfound complexity

She manages to cover the obscure 1850 best seller The Wide, Wide World as well as Judy Blume’s Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret , along with critical essays from thinkers such as Hilton Als and Saidiya Hartman; each volume mentioned is worth tracking down

So are other volumes in the series this belongs to, NYU Press’s Avidly Reads. — Sophia Stewart From our list: What to read to wake up your brain Out Next Week 📚 Profiles in Cowardice , by Jacob Weisberg 📚 Exit Party , by Emily St
John Mandel 📚 The Perilous Fight , by Colin Kaepernick Your Weekend Read A pool in California in 1984
Dorothy Bohm / Bridgeman Images A Great Novel Becomes a Bad Show By Jeremy Gordon For many readers, the career of the novelist Bret Easton Ellis is the standard for mainstream literary stardom

The biopic writes itself: While still a college undergraduate, Ellis strikes it big with his debut novel, 1985’s Less Than Zero , an unsentimental stenography of disaffected, privileged young adults in swanky Los Angeles
It’s soon adapted into a movie starring Robert Downey Jr. and James Spader, which itself bears little resemblance to the book

By the time he turns 30, he’s seemingly done it all: published multiple best sellers ( American Psycho , The Rules of Attraction ) filled with materialistic ennui, cheap sex, and lurid death; been mythologized as part of a literary “Brat Pack” alongside writers including Jay McInerney and Tama Janowitz; rubbed elbows with celebrities of the music and film worlds; made lots of money (for a writer, at least); and become addicted to drugs

title: Trump Loses the Other Strait
excerpt: As recently as last week, the Iran war appeared to be turning slightly in America’s favor
body: As recently as last week, the Iran war appeared to be turning slightly in America’s favor

The Houthis—the Yemen-based militia that is Iran’s most formidable remaining ally in the Middle East—were under pressure from their local rivals, and the Saudi air force was pounding them with air strikes

The president of Yemen’s internationally recognized government issued a triumphant statement declaring that the Houthis’ miscalculations “will open the door to their complete collapse.” With their Houthi partners wounded, Iran’s leaders would have one more reason to back down and agree to Donald Trump’s terms

Yesterday morning, those delusions drifted away like smoke as Houthi forces broke through their enemies’ defenses and seized the towns and islands around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the most important maritime choke points in the world
That loss leaves Trump, who had been hoping to win back control of the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, with a bitter surprise

His enemies now control both of the two important straits in the Middle East, through which a combined total of about a third of the world’s oil shipments pass every day. [ Read: An ‘America First’ deal with the Houthis ] It also underscores a stubborn fact: For all the setbacks suffered by Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” over the past year or two, its forces retain an ideological fervor and an esprit de corps that is sorely lacking on the other side
The Gulf states’ failure to work together against the Houthis has been catastrophic, and it echoes Trump’s own failure to devise a plausible or coordinated strategy against Iran

Although the Houthis already had the ability to threaten shipping in the Red Sea, the capture of the Bab el-Mandeb “means you can literally sit on the coast and fire at passing ships,” April Longley Alley, a Yemen expert at the Washington Institute on Near East Policy and the former political adviser to the United Nations special envoy for Yemen, told me. “It makes it easier and cheaper, and it solidifies, from a military and political point of view, that they have a stranglehold on the strait.” The United States might not be able to do much about this, even if the Pentagon launches a new round of air strikes on the Houthis. (The Saudi leader, Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman, called Trump twice yesterday urging him to strike the Houthis, Axios reported .) Bombs and missiles would achieve little without a ground force to take advantage of them, and America’s Yemeni allies are now battered and divided

The Trump administration waged a seven-week war against the group last year, and although it succeeded in killing some Houthi commanders, it did not dislodge the group or alter its ability to wage war, as Trump had promised
The Houthi advance is even worse news for Saudi Arabia
For many years, the Saudis have been struggling to tamp down the Houthi threat on its border
Now the Houthis have inherited a great deal of Saudi and Emirati supplies left behind by the official Yemeni government’s retreating forces
A video circulated yesterday of Mohammad Ali al-Houthi, one of the group’s top commanders and a cousin of its supreme leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, riding though Mokha in an Emirati armored vehicle
The mess that Saudi Arabia faces in Yemen is partly of its own making
The Houthis were born three decades ago in reaction to Saudi meddling in Yemen’s religious and political sphere

In December, tensions between the Saudi and Emirati leadership led Riyadh to demand that the Emiratis—their nominal allies—withdraw from Yemen, leaving the Saudis in charge of a patchwork of militias with divided loyalties

The various Yemeni factions continued to squabble among themselves even as their Houthi enemies were at the gates. “There was no coordination between commanders, between the intelligence and the drones, between the coast guard and the army—nothing,” Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at the think tank Chatham House, told me

The Houthis have clearly benefited from the Gulf’s disunity. “Last time the Houthis made a breakthrough at Marib in 2022, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia were able to jointly support a devastatingly effective Yemeni-government counterattack,” Michael Knights, the head of research at the consultancy Horizon Engage, told me

The Houthis, meanwhile, were disciplined and focused. “They sacrificed hundreds if not thousands of fighters,” a member of Yemen’s officially recognized government, who asked not to be identified for fear of repercussions, told me. “Our bullshit activists were putting out fake news about victories, while the Houthis were working in silence.” [ Read: Bombing the Houthis won’t work ] With the momentum on their side, the Houthis could now go on to seize more terrain in other parts of Yemen, including Marib province, where much of Yemen’s oil is located
They could also extend their power bloodlessly, by cutting deals with tribal and regional leaders in the south and east
All of this would further consolidate their power and strengthen their Iranian patrons
The Houthi victories have already put into doubt the value of the Mecca Alliance, the mutual-defense pact formed in August by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey
Islamabad and Ankara have shown no inclination to help the Saudis, despite a rash of recent Houthi strikes on targets in southern Saudi Arabia
Iran’s vaunted Axis of Resistance is not a bulletproof covenant either
The Houthis were absent earlier this year when the United States and Israel started bombing Iran
But unlike their enemies, the Houthis and the Iranians have a deep ideological bond, one that their soldiers willingly die for
And the Houthis do not need to win every battle
As long as they can sink an occasional oil tanker, they will hold a whip hand over their Saudi neighbors, and over the rest of the world too.

title: The Download: biotech’s future and cheaper, cleaner steel
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

Meet the under-35s shaping the future of biotech Every year, MIT Technology Review puts together our 35 Innovators Under 35 , a list of some of the brightest and best young minds working across science and technology
This year’s honorees include nine people transforming biotech, whose work spans everything from lifesaving innovations to groundbreaking longevity tech

Their innovations include a “reprogramming” therapy that reverses vision loss, tiny brain electrodes inspired by Japanese art, and a personalized gene-editing treatment for a baby with a rare genetic disorder
There are even efforts to design new viruses with generative AI, which (hopefully) will produce new drugs or soak up pollution
Get to know the biotech innovators behind these breakthroughs . —Jessica Hamzelou This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter
Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday
Biotechnology is one of four categories in our 35 Innovators Under 35 list for 2026, featuring young people worldwide doing groundbreaking work in science and technology
Meet the rest of them here , or explore the full list across the AI, computing and robotics, biotechnology, and climate and energy categories
This founder is making cheaper, cleaner steel The steel industry isn’t exactly known for innovation
Very little has changed about purifying iron ore since the process was invented and commercialized in the 1850s
But Laureen Meroueh, founder of Hertha Metals, has an idea that could change that
Meroueh may have found a way to clean up steelmaking without driving up the price
Her new furnace turns iron ore into refined liquid steel in a single step and swaps coal for natural gas
Together, those changes slash emissions by at least half, she says, and cut costs by 25% compared with steelmaking as usual

Here’s how she plans to make steel cleaner without making it more expensive . —Bridget Reed Morawski Laureen Meroueh is one of the climate change and energy honorees on our 35 Innovators Under 35 list

The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Anthropic says it has blocked potential plots to build biological weapons The company identified five such cases. ( NYT $) + And six cases of using AI to build software for conventional weapons ( BBC ) + Governments are also using Claude for surveillance. ( Axios ) + While Russia-linked hackers used it to automate attacks on Ukraine. ( Quartz ) + The threats were revealed in a new Anthropic report. ( Guardian ) + Bill Gates says AI needs new guardrails . ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 California has banned addictive social media features for under-16s The law prohibits infinite scroll and autoplay. ( Guardian ) + It also introduces new rules for AI and companion chatbots. ( Reuters $) + It’s the first law of its kind in the US. ( NYT $) + Social media encourages the worst AI boosterism . ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 Two AI researchers have left Anthropic and Google over safety risks They left a day after Jacob Coxon’s viral departure from Anthropic. ( NBC News ) + Elon Musk called their concerns a “setup” and a “psyop.” ( Guardian ) + AI fears are pushing Congress toward tougher regulation. ( WSJ $) 4 Sam Altman is pitching OpenAI’s cyber defenses to power companies The meetings followed reports of AI attacks on critical systems. ( Politico $) + Altman also told staff that OpenAI is open to slowing down AI

Bloomberg $) 5 After years of fighting AI, music labels are starting to embrace it Universal is partnering with ElevenLabs on an AI remix platform.( Gizmodo ) + AI is complicating definitions of creativity . ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Chinese drugmakers are challenging US dominance in weight-loss drugs They’re developing hundreds of GLP-1 treatments for global markets. ( WSJ $) 7 Electric air taxis have begun official test flights in Texas They’re the first flights under the White House’s new pilot program. ( Verge ) 8 Chinese drones are helping to rescue survivors of Nepal’s floods They’re delivering food and airlifting bodies from flood-hit areas. ( Ars Technica ) 9 NASA and IBM have built an AI model to map the moon It could help locate ice and identify safer landing sites. ( Register ) 10 One man is on a quest to digitally preserve America’s public restrooms His Restroom Archive is a museum-style repository of 3D scans. ( 404 Media ) Quote of the day “ I didn’t ask Facebook to build a profile of my family—I posted a video of me singing in the car with my kids.”  —Kalie Roberts, a travel content creator, says in an Instagram reel that Meta AI used years of Facebook posts to piece together her children’s identities and pinpoint where her family lives

One more thing Chinese tech workers are starting to train their AI doubles—and pushing back In April, a GitHub project called Colleague Skill struck a nerve by claiming to “distill” a worker’s skills and personality—and replicate them with an AI agent
Though the project was a spoof, it prompted a wave of soul-searching among otherwise enthusiastic early adopters
A number of tech workers told MIT Technology Review that their bosses are already encouraging them to document their workflows for automation via tools like OpenClaw
Many now fear that they are being flattened into code and losing their professional identity
In response, some are fighting back with tools designed to sabotage the automation process

Read the full story on their battle with clone workers . —Caiwei Chen We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + Worried about Flock cameras? These guys designed a car to fool them. + Webb’s Near-Infrared Camera has captured a galactic merger’s dazzling final phase . + An exquisitely preserved 66-million-year-old bird feather was found in a fossilised dinosaur dropping. + A plucky preservationist travelled 1,700 miles and made 52 calls from a rare phone box to keep it in service.

title: Meet the under-35s shaping the future of biotech
excerpt: Saving mothers with a $70 device: Tanzanian innovator Paschal Kija developed Mkanda Salama, a low-cost wrap that stopped dangerous postpartum bleeding in 73% of
body: Saving mothers with a $70 device: Tanzanian innovator Paschal Kija developed Mkanda Salama, a low-cost wrap that stopped dangerous postpartum bleeding in 73% of women within 20 minutes—targeting a complication behind nearly a third of maternal deaths in Tanzania

Brain electrodes inspired by paper art: Xiao Yang is designing ultra-small, flexible electrodes that mimic actual neurons, including a kirigami-inspired honeycomb spiral sheet—potentially reducing brain tissue damage while advancing how scientists study neurological activity

AI-designed viruses that actually work: Samuel King used generative AI to create genetic blueprints for entirely new bacteriophages, then printed them as DNA strands—and they replicated, burst from bacterial cells, and infected neighboring bacteria, hinting at future uses in medicine or pollution cleanup

Turning back the clock on aging cells: Ryan Lu's reprogramming therapy reversed vision loss in aged, blind mice—and now an almost identical version is being tested in humans, with a biotech company dosing its first volunteer in June. " data-chronoton-post-id="1143834" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Every year, MIT Technology Review puts together a list of some of the brightest and best young minds working across science and technology
Our 35 Innovators Under 35 are the ones to watch—people whose research and technical work stands to shape the future of their fields
This year, the list includes nine people who are transforming biotech
And this week, I’m going to give you a taste of some of the very cool stuff five of them are working on, which includes lifesaving innovations and groundbreaking “age reversal” tech.   1

Preventing maternal deaths Let’s start with Paschal Kija, a 28-year-old who has developed a device to treat postpartum hemorrhage—a dangerous birth complication that contributes to around 29% of maternal deaths in his home country, Tanzania
The Mkanda Salama (“Safe Wrap” in Swahili) is easy to use and costs just $70
A study found that it stopped postpartum bleeding in 73% of women within 20 minutes. 2
Making brain electrodes inspired by Japanese art For decades, scientists have been developing, testing, and implanting brain electrodes

These devices are literally inserted into people’s brains, so while they can help us understand brain activity and treat various neurological disorders, it’s not totally surprising that they can also cause a bit of damage
Xiao Yang, 34, is working on ultra-small electrodes, which she hopes will have less of an impact on surrounding brain tissue
Her electrodes are flexible, too—in fact, they look a lot like actual neurons
Yang is also creating sheets of electrodes to study brain cells in the lab
Inspired by kirigami—the traditional Japanese art of cutting paper to form three-dimensional shapes—she’s created a sheet of electrodes with a honeycombed structure shaped like a spiral basket
And she’s already using it to study brain cells. 3
Developing an all-new treatment for baby KJ In 2024, Kyle “KJ” Muldoon Jr. was born with a rare and potentially fatal genetic disorder
Sarah Grandinette was a member of a team that developed an entirely new, personalized treatment for him—a gene-editing therapy essentially designed to correct a genetic misspelling
Grandinette, who is now 26, created cells with KJ’s genetic variant and used them to screen gene-editing approaches; then she tested potential medicines in mice and monkeys
KJ ultimately got his first dose of the resulting treatment when he was about seven months old
He responded well and was eventually discharged from hospital
Reversing the aging process to treat eye disease The buzziest tech in longevity right now centers on reprogramming—attempts to rewind the age of cells by resetting them to a more embryonic-like state
In a study published in 2020, Yuancheng (Ryan) Lu (now 34) and his colleagues showed that a reprogramming therapy reversed vision loss in aged, blind mice
Now an almost identical version of that therapy is being tested in people with eye disease
Life Biosciences, the company developing the drug, dosed its first volunteer in June. 5
Using AI to design new viruses Last year, Samuel King used a generative AI model to come up with new genetic blueprints for bacteriophages —teeny viruses that can infect bacteria
Once he had those blueprints, he printed them out as strands of DNA
In experiments, he found that those AI-designed viruses could create new copies of themselves, burst out of bacterial cells, and infect other nearby bacteria
Viruses aren’t alive, but King, 27, hopes that AI-designed life forms might one day be used to make drugs or soak up pollution

title: How anti-bribery laws apply to Trump’s promise of $5,000 payments if Republicans keep control of Congress
url:
<title>How anti-bribery laws apply to Trump’s promise of $5,000 payments if Republicans keep control of Congress</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759374/original/file-20260911-50-3skz6w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=43%2C0%2C4233%2C2822&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">President Donald Trump speaks at the RNC midterm convention in Dallas on Sept. 9, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election2026Republicans/28edb16b54864df889e79080c8f43c6c/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=President%20Trump&amp;currentItemNo=85&amp;startingItemNo=750&amp;sourceLocation=Search">Eric Lee/Pool photo via AP</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://www.houstonpublicmedia.org/articles/news/politics/election-2026/2026/09/10/561450/trump-promises-5000-dividend-in-convention-speech-but-only-if-republicans-win/">In his keynote address</a> to the Republican midterm convention on Sept. 9, 2026, <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/10/trump-dividend-midterms-gop.html">President Donald Trump promised</a> that if Republicans retain control of Congress in November, he <a href="https://time.com/article/2026/09/10/trump-dividend-five-thousand-dollars-midterms-republican-convention/">would authorize a US$5,000 payment to every American adult</a>. </p>

<p>Trump’s offer seems to run afoul of federal laws, which make it <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/597">a crime to pay for votes</a>.</p>

<p>After Trump’s speech, <a href="https://x.com/samstein/status/2097870389489594746">political commentator Sam Stein posted</a> on X: “trump openly bribing people to vote for republicans. $5k per person if republicans hold the house and the senate?” </p>

<p>Stein was not alone in referencing bribery. Lisa Gilbert, co-president of Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy group, <a href="https://www.citizen.org/news/trumps-desperate-attempt-to-bribe-voters-ahead-of-election-is-a-new-low/">issued the following statement after Trump’s speech</a>: “Trump knows he can’t do this, and yet he’s attempting to bribe voters with the false promise of cash to help his party win an election.”</p>

<p>But as a <a href="https://press.umich.edu/Books/T/The-Rhetoric-of-Law">scholar of political and legal rhetoric</a>, I think it’s worth further examining what the president said and whether his promise violated any law.</p>

<h2>An American tradition</h2>

<p>Paying voters to support a particular candidate, or promising government jobs in exchange for votes, <a href="https://live-sas-www-history.pantheon.sas.upenn.edu/publications/2016/mary-frances-berry">has a long history</a> in the United States. <a href="https://billofrightsinstitute.org/essays/william-boss-tweed-and-political-machines/">It was a staple</a> of <a href="https://politicaldictionary.com/words/machine-politics/">machine politics</a> in big cities starting in the late 19th century. </p>

<p>The political scholar <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055408080106">Simeon Nichter argues</a> that it would be better to describe these practices as examples of “turnout buying.” <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055408080106">He notes</a> that “observers in various U.S. cities have complained that some politicians use ‘street money’ – small, unreported cash payments ostensibly used for legal get-out-the-vote efforts such as canvassing and transporting voters – as direct payments for turnout.”</p>

<p>What Nichter describes has made a comeback in our era.</p>

<p>Recall <a href="https://abc7news.com/story/elon-musk-broke-law-promising-voters-1-million-payouts-wisconsin-board-says/19515645/">Elon Musk’s effort to ensure a Republican victory</a> in a 2025 state Supreme Court election in Wisconsin. He spent millions in that effort and, as <a href="https://www.ap.org/news-highlights/elections/2026/elon-musk-likely-broke-the-law-by-promising-voters-1-million-payouts-wisconsin-board-says/">The Associated Press reported</a>, offered “$1 million to people who voted in the Supreme Court election” to encourage them to vote.</p>

<p>In July 2026, the Wisconsin Elections Commission <a href="https://apnews.com/article/elon-musk-wisconsin-election-million-dollar-checks-2900f27acc373c9f1661a934f00c0c3d">found enough evidence to refer</a> citizen complaints about Musk’s behavior to a district attorney, “which can choose,” as the AP notes, “to bring criminal charges over violating the state law against election bribery.” </p>

<p>A month later, a state prosecutor said he could <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/elon-musk-wont-face-election-bribery-charges-in-wisconsin-state-prosecutor-says/">not prove Musk’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt</a> and would not bring charges.</p>

<h2>Federal law</h2>

<p>Because state and federal laws differ, we can’t extrapolate from the Wisconsin decision to Trump’s $5,000 promise.</p>

<p>Two provisions of federal law relating to vote buying <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/597">were adopted by Congress</a> and became law in 1948. Both treated that practice as a form of election interference.</p>

<p>The first <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/597">reads as follows</a>: “Whoever makes or offers to make an expenditure to any person, either to vote or withhold his vote, or to vote for or against any candidate; and whoever solicits, accepts, or receives any such expenditure in consideration of his vote or the withholding of his vote; Shall be fined under this title or imprisoned … or both.”</p>

<p>The second <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/600">prohibits offering government benefits</a> “to any person as consideration, favor, or reward for any political activity or for the support of or opposition to any candidate or any political party in connection with any … election to any political office.”</p>

<p>Both provisions focus on the use of money or the promise of benefits to get individuals to vote in a particular way.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man in suit and tie shakes hands with women dress in red and white." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759375/original/file-20260911-70-b816kw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">President Trump arrives at the Republican convention in Dallas on Sept. 9, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Election2026Republicans/009ed2b88d3348e7a06ee52810941f9e/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=President%20Trump&amp;currentItemNo=90&amp;startingItemNo=850&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>But Trump did not make his offer to any particular voter or set of voters. And, unlike Musk, he was acting as a public figure. The president’s promise was directed to all voters, not just to those who vote Republican.</p>

<p>John Day, a former federal prosecutor, compared Trump’s “dividend” to <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/10/us/politics/trump-dividend-5000-check.html">a pledge to deliver a tax break</a>. “A promise to lower taxes also gives voters a financial reason to support a candidate, but that does not, by itself, make the promise a bribe,” Day told The New York Times.</p>

<h2>Supreme Court precedent</h2>

<p>In 1982, in Brown v. Hartlage, the Supreme Court <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/456/45/">weighed in on the legality of political figures</a> promising financial benefits to voters. It found nothing wrong with the practice so long as the benefit was not offered as a quid pro quo to a particular voter.</p>

<p>Writing for a unanimous court, Justice William Brennan said that a political candidate “no less than any other person, has a First Amendment right to engage in the discussion of public issues and vigorously and tirelessly to advocate his own election and the election of other candidates.” </p>

<p>In his view, that right includes making statements about financial gains voters might receive if a candidate or a party wins an election, as long as they were “made openly and were subject to the criticism of his political opponent and to the scrutiny of the voters.” Such statements, Brennan added, were different from “corrupting private agreements and solicitations historically recognized as unprotected by the First Amendment.”</p>

<p>The Hartlage decision remains the applicable precedent today.</p>

<p>A year after the court’s decision, however, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/scer.2.1147126">legal scholars Peter Aranson and Kenneth Shepsle argued</a> that the Supreme Court decision countered several lower court decisions that had treated promises of the kind the high court approved “as analogous to bribes, which would turn the citizenry’s attention away from ‘proper’ public policy issues.”</p>

<p>Trump may view the question of whether Republicans retain control of Congress as just such an issue.</p>

<h2>Beyond legality</h2>

<p>Whatever Trump’s view, <a href="https://www.aei.org/commentary/the-transactional-trap/">commentators have observed</a> that in Trump’s world, relationships are transactional. It is the deal that counts, not the values it promotes or undermines. So, the importance of Trump’s cash offer goes beyond the legal question of whether it is bribery, vote buying or a legitimate political promise. </p>

<p>It’s worth focusing attention on the virtues and vices of the transactional approach to politics, what it does to the character of U.S. political life and to the way Americans see the world.</p>

<p>One of Trump’s critics, the <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2025/03/political-enemy-retribution-efforts/682095/">former presidential speechwriter Peter Wehner</a>, describes what he calls “the great civic danger posed by Donald Trump” this way: “that the habits of his heart become the habits of our hearts: that his code of conduct becomes ours.”</p>

<p>Whether or not he is right, Wehner points Americans to a domain beyond law as the right place to assess the president’s promise of a “<a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6081944-trump-dividend-pledge-backlash/">Trump Dividend</a>.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291722/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Eric Lee/Pool photo via AP In his keynote address to the Republican midterm convention on Sept. 9, 2026, President Donald Trump promised that if Republicans retain control of Congress in November, he would authorize a US$5,000 payment to every American adult
Trump’s offer seems to run afoul of federal laws, which make it a crime to pay for votes

After Trump’s speech, political commentator Sam Stein posted on X: “trump openly bribing people to vote for republicans. $5k per person if republicans hold the house and the senate?” Stein was not alone in referencing bribery

Lisa Gilbert, co-president of Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy group, issued the following statement after Trump’s speech : “Trump knows he can’t do this, and yet he’s attempting to bribe voters with the false promise of cash to help his party win an election.” But as a scholar of political and legal rhetoric , I think it’s worth further examining what the president said and whether his promise violated any law
An American tradition Paying voters to support a particular candidate, or promising government jobs in exchange for votes, has a long history in the United States
It was a staple of machine politics in big cities starting in the late 19th century

The political scholar Simeon Nichter argues that it would be better to describe these practices as examples of “turnout buying.” He notes that “observers in various U.S. cities have complained that some politicians use ‘street money’ – small, unreported cash payments ostensibly used for legal get-out-the-vote efforts such as canvassing and transporting voters – as direct payments for turnout.” What Nichter describes has made a comeback in our era
Recall Elon Musk’s effort to ensure a Republican victory in a 2025 state Supreme Court election in Wisconsin
He spent millions in that effort and, as The Associated Press reported , offered “$1 million to people who voted in the Supreme Court election” to encourage them to vote

In July 2026, the Wisconsin Elections Commission found enough evidence to refer citizen complaints about Musk’s behavior to a district attorney, “which can choose,” as the AP notes, “to bring criminal charges over violating the state law against election bribery.” A month later, a state prosecutor said he could not prove Musk’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt and would not bring charges
Federal law Because state and federal laws differ, we can’t extrapolate from the Wisconsin decision to Trump’s $5,000 promise
Two provisions of federal law relating to vote buying were adopted by Congress and became law in 1948
Both treated that practice as a form of election interference

The first reads as follows : “Whoever makes or offers to make an expenditure to any person, either to vote or withhold his vote, or to vote for or against any candidate; and whoever solicits, accepts, or receives any such expenditure in consideration of his vote or the withholding of his vote; Shall be fined under this title or imprisoned … or both.” The second prohibits offering government benefits “to any person as consideration, favor, or reward for any political activity or for the support of or opposition to any candidate or any political party in connection with any … election to any political office.” Both provisions focus on the use of money or the promise of benefits to get individuals to vote in a particular way
President Trump arrives at the Republican convention in Dallas on Sept. 9, 2026
AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson But Trump did not make his offer to any particular voter or set of voters
And, unlike Musk, he was acting as a public figure
The president’s promise was directed to all voters, not just to those who vote Republican

John Day, a former federal prosecutor, compared Trump’s “dividend” to a pledge to deliver a tax break . “A promise to lower taxes also gives voters a financial reason to support a candidate, but that does not, by itself, make the promise a bribe,” Day told The New York Times
Supreme Court precedent In 1982, in Brown v
Hartlage, the Supreme Court weighed in on the legality of political figures promising financial benefits to voters
It found nothing wrong with the practice so long as the benefit was not offered as a quid pro quo to a particular voter

Writing for a unanimous court, Justice William Brennan said that a political candidate “no less than any other person, has a First Amendment right to engage in the discussion of public issues and vigorously and tirelessly to advocate his own election and the election of other candidates.” In his view, that right includes making statements about financial gains voters might receive if a candidate or a party wins an election, as long as they were “made openly and were subject to the criticism of his political opponent and to the scrutiny of the voters.” Such statements, Brennan added, were different from “corrupting private agreements and solicitations historically recognized as unprotected by the First Amendment.” The Hartlage decision remains the applicable precedent today

A year after the court’s decision, however, legal scholars Peter Aranson and Kenneth Shepsle argued that the Supreme Court decision countered several lower court decisions that had treated promises of the kind the high court approved “as analogous to bribes, which would turn the citizenry’s attention away from ‘proper’ public policy issues.” Trump may view the question of whether Republicans retain control of Congress as just such an issue
Beyond legality Whatever Trump’s view, commentators have observed that in Trump’s world, relationships are transactional
It is the deal that counts, not the values it promotes or undermines
So, the importance of Trump’s cash offer goes beyond the legal question of whether it is bribery, vote buying or a legitimate political promise
It’s worth focusing attention on the virtues and vices of the transactional approach to politics, what it does to the character of U.S. political life and to the way Americans see the world

One of Trump’s critics, the former presidential speechwriter Peter Wehner , describes what he calls “the great civic danger posed by Donald Trump” this way: “that the habits of his heart become the habits of our hearts: that his code of conduct becomes ours.” Whether or not he is right, Wehner points Americans to a domain beyond law as the right place to assess the president’s promise of a “ Trump Dividend .” Austin Sarat does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

<title>Here’s how teachers and parents can collaborate and help Michigan’s 1.4M students succeed</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754711/original/file-20260818-50-49qtqj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1697%2C5821%2C3881&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Family engagement can help students regularly attend classes, according to researchers. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=michigan%20students%20&amp;mediaType=photo">Paul Sancya/AP</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>About <a href="https://www.mischooldata.org/student-enrollment-counts-report/">1.4 million Michigan students</a> returned to the state’s K-12 public school classrooms this fall. </p>

<p>One of the most powerful influences on how these students will perform exists outside the classroom: the quality of the partnerships that schools and families establish with each other. </p>

<p>Establishing these partnerships may be easier than it sounds. Throughout more than four decades as an educator and <a href="https://education.msu.edu/people/e/edwards-patricia">researcher studying literacy and family engagement</a>, I have learned that most families deeply care about their children’s education and want to work with teachers toward the best possible outcomes.</p>

<h2>Family engagement helps students achieve</h2>

<p>This message is especially timely in Michigan. Many students continue to experience challenges in reading following the COVID-19 pandemic. Only <a href="https://www.mischooldata.org/grades-3-8-state-testing-includes-psat-data-performance/">39% of Michigan third graders</a> scored proficient or advanced in English language arts on the M-STEP, an annual state exam, in the 2024-25 school year.</p>

<p>In 2024, Michigan students scored below the national average in reading on the <a href="https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/">National Assessment of Educational Progress</a>. Michigan fourth graders <a href="https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/profiles/stateprofile/overview/mi?cti=PgTab_Findings&amp;sub=MAT&amp;chort=1&amp;year=2024R3&amp;st=MN&amp;sfj=NP&amp;sj=MI&amp;fs=Grade">averaged 209</a>, five points below the national average, while eighth graders averaged 255, compared with 257 nationally.</p>

<p>Although standardized test scores <a href="https://www.nea.org/student-success/standardized-testing-student-assessment">do not fully capture the breadth of students’ knowledge</a>, abilities or potential, they can provide <a href="https://nces.ed.gov/">one useful indicator</a> of how well students are developing literacy skills. </p>

<p><a href="https://bealearninghero.org/">National</a> <a href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA1108-8.html">studies</a> also demonstrate that families want to play active roles in their children’s education. They show, too, that many parents seek clearer communication and more meaningful opportunities to collaborate with educators. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Shelves filled with books inside a school library" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757927/original/file-20260904-60-jro6n8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Michigan students’ low literacy rates point to a need for more support.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/new-reading-space-is-seen-after-the-renovation-by-macys-and-news-photo/1649095008?adppopup=true">Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images for Macy's Inc.</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In my assessment, one of the most encouraging developments in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/1361332052000341006">family engagement research</a> over the past two decades has been the growing recognition among researchers, educators and schools that parents are not simply volunteers who occasionally assist schools. They are co-educators whose knowledge, cultural wealth and lived experiences enrich children’s educational opportunities. </p>

<p>This understanding reflects <a href="https://www.ed.gov/sites/ed/files/documents/family-community/partners-education.pdf">a broader movement</a> toward educational equity and shared responsibility for student success.</p>

<h2>Parents are partners in education</h2>

<p>Families may be invited to attend conferences, literacy nights or workshops, but they are not always invited to share their knowledge or participate as equal partners in decisions about their children’s learning. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Woman stand behind boy sitting at desk." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756634/original/file-20260827-50-7oznu7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Families and educators who work together can help students develop stronger literacy skills.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=back%20to%20school%20michigan&amp;mediaType=photo">Paul Sancya/AP Photo</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In my experience, families may feel that educators do not understand their cultural and linguistic practices. They may notice that communication flows primarily from school to home rather than in both directions, or that their knowledge of their own children is undervalued.</p>

<p>For families whose previous encounters with schools have involved judgment, exclusion or racism, or educators focusing on perceived shortcomings rather than recognizing families’ strengths, an invitation to participate does not automatically create understanding.</p>

<p>Some of my most formative lessons came during my early work with African American families in Louisiana. I began spending time with parents and listening carefully to what they understood schools were asking them to do at home. </p>

<p>Teachers frequently encouraged parents to “read to your child,” without explaining what meaningful reading might look like. </p>

<p>Some parents were uncertain about teachers’ expectations or viewed reading primarily as getting the words right. These experiences helped inspire <a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/Parents_as_Partners_in_Reading/u4p7PQAACAAJ?hl=en">Parents as Partners in Reading</a>, a program I designed to help families support children’s literacy through interactive read-alouds that encourage conversation and making connections between books and children’s everyday lives. </p>

<p>In Louisiana, I showed rather than simply told them how they might make reading with their children more interactive and enjoyable. I modeled how to sit comfortably with a child, let the child hold the book and turn the pages, vary their voices, pause to ask questions, talk together about the pictures and follow the child’s interests and reactions. </p>

<p>Rather than prescribing a single “right” way to read together, these interactions gave parents opportunities to try different approaches, ask questions and discover what worked best for them and their children.</p>

<p>Parents then practiced these approaches with one another before using them. As their confidence increased, the interactions began to flow more naturally: Parents relied less on the strategies I had modeled and became more comfortable following their children’s lead, responding to their questions and comments and allowing conversations about the story to develop spontaneously. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Students and parents reading books while sitting at a desk." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757929/original/file-20260904-50-4gw8u1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757929/original/file-20260904-50-4gw8u1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757929/original/file-20260904-50-4gw8u1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757929/original/file-20260904-50-4gw8u1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757929/original/file-20260904-50-4gw8u1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757929/original/file-20260904-50-4gw8u1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757929/original/file-20260904-50-4gw8u1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Educators can learn from families about what their children’s interests and strengths are.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/parents-read-books-to-their-children-during-a-program-with-news-photo/1258959248?adppopup=true">Salwan Georges/The Washington Post via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Talking to families with empathy</h2>

<p>I’ve watched educators transform their relationships with families once they begin viewing parents through their strengths rather than perceived flaws. Families know dimensions of their children that may never be visible during the school day: the child who loves to tell stories at the dinner table, or the child who is fascinated by cars or animals.</p>

<p>When educators listen to those stories, they gain information that can change how they understand and teach a child. Family engagement must also mean creating opportunities for educators to learn from families.</p>

<p>Instead of asking why families are not involved, they begin asking <a href="https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED474521">how schools can become more welcoming</a>, more responsive and more collaborative. That shift in perspective often changes the entire culture of a school.</p>

<p>Here are a few ways educators can build relationships with families and vice versa:</p>

<p><strong>Build relationships before you need them</strong></p>

<p>Teachers shouldn’t wait until there is a problem to reach out to families. Relationships are strongest when schools communicate with families before challenges arise. </p>

<p>A welcoming phone call, a quick note celebrating something a child did well, an invitation to visit the classroom, or simply taking time to learn about a child’s interests can go a long way. </p>

<p>Parents can make a point of introducing themselves to their child’s teacher early in the school year. Parents might share something the teacher would find helpful to know about their child – what excites them, what they enjoy reading or doing at home, or what helps them feel confident as learners. </p>

<p>These early exchanges also communicate an important message: “I know my child in ways that can help you teach them, and I want us to work together.” </p>

<p><strong>Make communication a conversation</strong></p>

<p>Families should hear from educators, but educators also need to hear from families. Communication is most meaningful when educators listen as much as they inform. </p>

<p>Educators can ask parents and caregivers: What are your hopes for your child this year? What should I know about your child that will help me be a better teacher? How does your child learn best? What is the easiest way for us to stay in touch?</p>

<p>Parents can ask teachers: “What are you noticing about my child as a reader and learner?” and “What are some things we can do at home that would reinforce what you are teaching at school?” </p>

<p><strong>Bring empathy to difficult conversations</strong></p>

<p>At some point, educators may need to talk with families about academic, behavioral or attendance concerns. Teachers can begin by sharing what the child does well and listening to what the family is seeing at home. Then invite their insights and perspectives: “Here is what I’m noticing. What are you seeing, and how can we work together?” This small shift – from presenting families with a problem to inviting them into a conversation – can transform a potentially difficult exchange into an opportunity for genuine partnership.</p>

<p>Families can listen carefully when teachers raise concerns and ask questions to better understand what the teacher is observing about their child. They can also share what they notice about their child at home, since children may demonstrate different strengths, behaviors and abilities in different settings. </p>

<p>Together, families and teachers can identify strategies to try at home and at school to address the concern and agree on a time to reconnect and discuss the child’s progress.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/287763/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: CDC vs. Pennsylvania: Why conflicting public health messages jeopardize public safety
