<title>CDC vs. Pennsylvania: Why conflicting public health messages jeopardize public safety</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759220/original/file-20260910-50-jh1jbg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6617%2C4411&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Pennsylvania has seen more than 600 cases of measles in 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/measles-blood-test-conceptual-image-royalty-free-image/1307404002">Science Photo Library via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>If you’ve been following the dispute between Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., you probably know that it centers on the <a href="https://politifact.com/article/2026/sep/01/timeline-measles-deaths-pennslvania-rfk-shapiro/">deaths of two infants in Lancaster County</a> in late August 2026.</p>

<p>And you may be aware that despite the <a href="https://www.statnews.com/2026/09/09/coroner-details-infant-deaths-pennsylvania-measles-outbreak/">county coroner’s confirmation</a> that one infant died due to measles, while the other’s death was “measles-associated,” the <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html">measles dashboard</a> on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website counts neither death as of Sept. 10.</p>

<p>It’s easy to dismiss the squabble as political posturing between public officials. But as an <a href="https://publichealth.uic.edu/profiles/wallace-katrine/">epidemiologist</a> who studies <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=B5DbbcgAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">vaccine-preventable illnesses and health communication</a>, I worry that for people seeking accurate information about how to keep their families safe – in this case, families in Lancaster County – there’s an enormous cost when health authorities no longer speak in one voice. </p>

<p>In the confusion that such rifts create, the public has no way of knowing which disagreements are about evidence and which are driven by ideology and narrative control.</p>



<h2>Deaths in dispute</h2>

<p>The U.S. government issues a certificate for every death, confirming its <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/writing-cause-of-death-statements.htm">underlying cause</a> following a physician’s examination. The death certificate poses a narrow question: What single condition set in motion the chain of events that ended in this person’s death? This is recorded as the cause of death. </p>

<p>Because measles is what the CDC calls a <a href="https://www.medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001929.htm">notifiable condition, or a reportable disease</a>, measles deaths get added to a national count. Contributing conditions go on a separate line in the document and are not counted. </p>

<p>Nobody disputes that both infants had measles when they died. The argument is which line on the death certificate “measles” belongs on. The Pennsylvania Department of Health <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/newsroom/pennsylvania-department-of-health-confirms-two-measles-associate">has called both deaths measles-associated</a>. This term is used when there’s evidence the person had measles, but there’s no settled official cause of death yet. It’s a holding category, not a verdict.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759225/original/file-20260910-50-q82aq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Gloved hands of a medical professional examine a rash on a child's chest." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759225/original/file-20260910-50-q82aq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759225/original/file-20260910-50-q82aq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759225/original/file-20260910-50-q82aq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759225/original/file-20260910-50-q82aq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759225/original/file-20260910-50-q82aq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759225/original/file-20260910-50-q82aq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759225/original/file-20260910-50-q82aq7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">The CDC is tasked with keeping an accurate tally of measles cases and deaths.</span>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The job of determining the official cause – that is, certifying a death – falls to the county coroner. Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni concluded that for one of the infants, a newborn boy who died in mid-August, <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/pennsylvania-measles-infant-coroner-says-ruptured-spleen-rcna594793">the cause was a ruptured spleen</a> unrelated to the measles infection. For a 6-week-old girl who died Aug. 18, <a href="https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/measles/lancaster-county-coroner-confirms-second-measles-death-also-involves-child">he found that measles was the cause</a>. </p>

<p>These are not competing conclusions. They come from two different systems asking two different questions. County coroners’ decisions on cause of death are legal finding, made one case at a time, that feed <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db548.htm">national vital statistics</a>. </p>

<p>State health departments, on the other hand, run disease surveillance. They track who got sick and who died during an outbreak so they can contain it. Surveillance moves in days because it has to; death certification moves in weeks because it should. The two rarely line up in real time.</p>

<h2>A moving target</h2>

<p>While the apparent divergence between county and state data was basically a technicality, the exchange between Shapiro and Kennedy was more of a brawl.  </p>

<p>Shapiro <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HeXrr9d9f3A">announced the infants’ deaths on Aug. 25</a> and blamed anti-vaccine rhetoric for falling vaccination rates and increasing cases. The CDC <a href="https://x.com/CDCgov/status/2092341381268115875">posted condolences on the social media platform X</a>, using Pennsylvania’s language calling the deaths measles-associated.</p>

<p>But in response, Kennedy suggested the <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/26/pennsylvania-outbreak-kennedy-measles-vax-01050922">deaths might have been fabricated</a> by a member of the governor’s staff. Two days after Shapiro’s announcement, the CDC <a href="https://x.com/CDCgov/status/2093065775070290082">walked back its post</a>, expressing appreciation for Kennedy’s efforts to clarify conflicting information from Pennsylvania officials about whether the two reported deaths were caused by measles.</p>

<p>Then, in an unusual move, on <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/31/measles-deaths-pennsylvania-excluded">Aug. 30</a>, the CDC changed the death count on its measles dashboard from 2 to an asterisk, with a footnote stating that the National Center for Health Statistics currently has no death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause.</p>

<p>No new evidence arrived in those two days that would explain the CDC’s new position.</p>

<p>HHS now says it is working with a national network of disease tracking experts on a <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html">standardized case definition</a> for measles deaths. Standard case definitions exist for measles infections but not for measles deaths, for the simple reason that until recently, dying from measles in the U.S. was an extremely rare occurrence: Between <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/wr/mm7414a1.htm">2001 and 2022</a>, the U.S. recorded roughly 4,000 cases and three deaths.</p>

<p>But writing a definition in the middle of a count – and applying it to a single state’s deaths – is a departure from protocol. Previously, during <a href="https://www.dshs.texas.gov/news-alerts/texas-announces-second-death-measles-outbreak">outbreaks in Texas</a> and <a href="https://www.nmhealth.org/news/alert/2025/3/?view=2188">New Mexico</a> in 2025, the CDC did <a href="https://www.statnews.com/2026/09/04/pennsylvania-measles-deaths-data-cdc-director-rfk-jr/">count three measles-associated deaths</a> while they were still being investigated. Declining to do so now <a href="https://www.statnews.com/2026/09/04/pennsylvania-measles-deaths-data-cdc-director-rfk-jr/">is inconsistent and confusing</a>, and breeds mistrust. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/6ZfjXab2mNU?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The Lancaster County coroner attributed one infant’s death to measles and the other’s death to a ruptured spleen.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Unnamed officials told news outlets that <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2026/08/31/new-cdc-director-delays-adding-pennsylvania-deaths-measles-data/">CDC Director Erica Schwartz removed the deaths</a> at <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/kennedy-asked-remove-pennsylvania-measles-death-cdc-tally-sources-say-2026-09-03/">Kennedy’s request</a>, after CDC staff had accepted the state’s data. HHS disputes this, and Kennedy said in a post on X that the coroner’s finding – that the newborn boy’s death was caused by a ruptured spleen – <a href="https://x.com/SecKennedy/status/2095972590808416484?s=20">vindicated federal caution</a>.</p>

<p>A parent sifting through all this information has no way to gauge who is right. The usual shortcut – check the CDC numbers on the measles dashboard – now yields an asterisk leading to a footnote that contradicts statements from state officials, a county coroner and the agency’s own condolence post from 10 days earlier. There’s no neutral tiebreaker left, which means the decision falls back on which institution you already trusted most.</p>

<h2>A broader split in public health guidance</h2>

<p>While that argument played out, a second rift was widening on a different track.</p>

<p>On Sept. 2, <a href="https://vaxintegrity.cidrap.umn.edu/2026-27-respiratory-season-evidence-review">four physician groups</a> – the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America – issued their own <a href="https://vaxintegrity.cidrap.umn.edu/2026-2027-respiratory-season-evidence-review-executive-summary">vaccine recommendations</a> for the fall respiratory season. </p>

<p>The pediatricians association had already <a href="https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/32835/AAP-releases-evidence-based-immunization-schedule">split from the CDC’s childhood immunization schedule in 2025</a>, ending a 30-year practice of publishing one agreed-upon set of recommendations for families. What’s new is that three more societies have now joined this public health separatist movement, and that the split has extended to the shots most adults get.</p>

<p>On influenza, the physician groups’ advice matches the CDC’s: Everyone 6 months and older should get a flu vaccine. On COVID-19 they go further, recommending vaccination for children 6 to 23 months, whereas the CDC tells parents to consult a doctor.</p>

<p>For decades, the CDC <a href="https://www.healio.com/news/pediatrics/20260904/physicians-publish-fall-vaccine-guidance-filling-void-left-by-cdc">has issued fall vaccine recommendations</a> each year, offering a unified slate of federal advice for everyone across the U.S. to follow. Now, with the federal advisory <a href="https://theconversation.com/rfk-jrs-shakeup-of-vaccine-advisory-committee-raises-worries-about-scientific-integrity-of-health-recommendations-258674">committee that makes those recommendations sidelined</a> and <a href="https://theconversation.com/federal-judge-temporarily-blocks-rfk-jr-s-vaccine-agenda-an-epidemiologist-answers-questions-parents-may-have-278709">embroiled in a legal battle</a>, the agency has issued no new federal vaccine guidance for this season. The four physician groups stepped forward to fill the gap. </p>

<p>Yet technically, the CDC’s previous seasonal recommendations – and its revised childhood immunization schedule – still stand, creating a confusing doubling of critical health guidance.   </p>

<h2>The cost of fracture</h2>

<p>This confusion has a measurable cost. </p>

<p>Measles is among the <a href="https://theconversation.com/measles-is-one-of-the-deadliest-and-most-contagious-infectious-diseases-and-one-of-the-most-easily-preventable-224493">most contagious</a> diseases known. Roughly <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/signs-symptoms/index.html">1 to 3 in 1,000</a> children who catch it die, and in 2025, <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html">11% of cases</a> required a hospital stay. A 2025 study put the <a href="https://publichealth.jhu.edu/ivac/2025/estimating-the-financial-costs-of-measles-outbreaks">average cost at roughly US$43,000 per case</a>. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html">national case count reached 3,134</a> on Sept. 4, the highest since 1991. As of the same date, Pennsylvania <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles">had recorded 624 cases</a> – 91 in the previous week. More than 40% of Pennsylvania’s cases have been in Lancaster County.</p>

<p>Parents must now reconcile a recently revised federal immunization schedule, a set of physician-society recommendations that departs from it, a state count of two deaths and a national count of none. </p>

<p>Each of those positions has an institution behind it. None of them explains how it relates to the others – and that is what’s most damaging. Public trust doesn’t only collapse when officials lie. It erodes when people are handed different information that can’t be squared, or misleading information, and are left to sort it out alone.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291239/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>‘The Uprising’ shows how medieval people weren’t so obedient after all</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759204/original/file-20260910-50-31ttg1.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=171%2C92%2C1799%2C1199&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Woody Norman as King Richard II in &#39;The Uprising,&#39; which tells the story of the 1381 Peasants&#39; Revolt, a major uprising across England that was triggered by high taxes and economic exploitation.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt36983905/mediaviewer/rm736427522/">Betina La Plante/Focus Features</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>For decades, I’ve been showing my medieval history students the “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/44S0sa6gWMM">autonomous collective</a>” scene from the 1975 film “<a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0071853/">Monty Python and the Holy Grail</a>.”</p>

<p>The clip is funny because it features two medieval peasants haranguing King Arthur while using the lexicon of a modern political Marxist. When Arthur explains that he was their king because the Lady of the Lake gave him Excalibur, one of the peasants objects: “Supreme executive power derives from a mandate from the masses, not from some farcical aquatic ceremony!”</p>

<p>It also subverts the assumption that medieval people were politically passive, with resistance to abuses of authority largely absent before the Renaissance and the Protestant Reformation.</p>

<p>But far from being an age of unquestioning obedience, <a href="https://www.britannica.com/event/Middle-Ages">the Middle Ages</a> – the period from roughly 500 to 1500 – witnessed a remarkable number of popular revolts and collective political action. </p>

<p>Even if they didn’t speak in the language of Karl Marx, ordinary people back then <a href="https://theconversation.com/medieval-europe-was-far-from-democratic-but-that-didnt-mean-tyrants-got-a-free-pass-227214">held strong views about the working of political authority</a>. And when they believed authorities had violated their obligations or lost their legitimacy, they routinely challenged rulers, bishops, tax collectors and urban elites.</p>

<h2>Enough is enough</h2>

<p>In the 11th and 12th centuries, <a href="https://muse-jhu-edu.uri.idm.oclc.org/book/100075">northern French peasants</a> famously resisted carrying out the work or paying the money that they owed to the lords who controlled the land they farmed.</p>

<p>But perhaps the most well-known insurrection is <a href="https://theconversation.com/uprisings-after-pandemics-have-happened-before-just-look-at-the-english-peasant-revolt-of-1381-139260">the English Peasants’ Revolt of 1381</a>, the subject of the new film “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZVkrhHebz1Q">The Uprising</a>,” starring Andrew Garfield.</p>

<p>After the first wave of the <a href="https://theconversation.com/uprisings-after-pandemics-have-happened-before-just-look-at-the-english-peasant-revolt-of-1381-139260">Black Death in 1348</a> created a massive labor shortage in Europe, workers <a href="https://www-jstor-org.uri.idm.oclc.org/stable/26422388">were better positioned to negotiate</a> for higher wages and better conditions. <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/social-sciences-and-humanities/serfdom">Serfs</a> – peasants bound to the land and subject to a lord’s authority – increasingly pushed back against oppressive feudal obligations. </p>

<p>But kings and lords resisted change. In 1351, England’s King Edward III decreed the <a href="https://avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/statlab.asp">Statute of Laborers</a>, which froze wages, derailing any aspiration for social mobility among the peasant class. Resentment continued to build with recurring episodes of the plague.</p>

<p>Then, in 1381, Edward’s grandson and successor – 12-year-old King Richard II – instituted a one-time <a href="https://www.1381.online/about/about_the_revolt/">tax of 12 pence</a> to raise funds for England’s ongoing war with France. Because the tax was charged per person rather than according to wealth, it placed a particularly heavy burden on poorer families.</p>

<p>The people had had enough: Crowds attacked tax collectors and eventually organized into a larger movement, burning houses, castles and the records that documented their obligations to their lords. They killed government officials before marching to London to confront the king.</p>

<p>The king met the rebels and pledged to abolish the poll tax and serfdom, while lowering the rent of agricultural land.</p>

<p>He later recanted those promises: His forces hunted down the rebels, quashing the uprising.</p>

            </figcaption>

<h2>A tradition of collective action</h2>

<p>Insurrections like the English Peasants’ Revolt erupted, in part, because in cities across Europe, regular people had cultivated a strong tradition of collective action. <a href="https://www.worldhistory.org/Medieval_Guilds/">There was broad membership in guilds</a>, which were voluntary associations of merchants and craftsmen. Then there were neighborhood <a href="https://www.medievalists.net/2021/11/medieval-confraternities-prayers-feasts-and-fees/">religious confraternities</a>, which were akin to today’s religious mutual-aid societies. Together, they gave ordinary townspeople networks through which they could organize around shared interests and grievances.</p>

<p>Over in France, the Hundred Years’ War caused a breakdown in authority. People were increasingly being asked to pay taxes they couldn’t afford. Unpaid troops routinely raided the countryside, and the French military suffered a number of significant military defeats.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759176/original/file-20260910-50-lhebba.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A colorful medieval-style illustration showing armed rebels attacking a fortified gate.             </figcaption>

<p>In 1358, <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-jacquerie-of-1358-9780198856412?cc=us&amp;lang=en&amp;">the Jacques</a> – a derogatory name for members of the lower French peasantry – razed noble estates and killed members of the aristocracy. They also joined forces with the Parisian bourgeoisie and the city’s chief political leader, Étienne Marcel, to fight for a greater voice in French government.</p>

<p>The rage underpinning the violence of what became known as the Jacquerie emerged from the fact that the same aristocracy that demanded so much of them could not fulfill their basic part of the bargain: protect them.</p>

<p>A little over a decade later, violence erupted in Florence, Italy. The city-state was an industrial juggernaut ruled by guilds, but their representatives all belonged to the urban elite. The lower classes of the textile industry weren’t represented by guilds and were largely disenfranchised. <a href="https://www.britannica.com/event/Revolt-of-the-Ciompi">So the Ciompi</a> – low-level woolworkers – demanded a role in the guild system. Those demands fell on deaf ears.</p>

<p>In June 1378, <a href="https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Popular_Revolutions_of_the_Late_Midd/BjNVEAAAQBAJ?hl=en&amp;gbpv=1&amp;printsec=frontcover">the Ciompi</a> revolted and attacked government offices. Thanks to their efforts, they won participation in the guild system for four years, up until the city’s old powerful merchant elite dissolved their lower guilds.</p>

<h2>Contesting the church</h2>

<p>Nor was the other main source of authority, the church, immune to attack.</p>

<p><a href="https://brill.com/display/title/14615?language=en&amp;srsltid=AfmBOoqUJiDIauUJaKFgastHj2VeWtlIqjjgW86_xjspAwoo8qqOptaQ">When power vacuums emerged</a> after the death of an abbot, bishop or even the pope, regular people routinely ransacked their property, taking with them a substantial amount of the dead’s movables. </p>

<p>As cardinal <a href="https://brill.com/display/title/14615?language=en&amp;srsltid=AfmBOoqUJiDIauUJaKFgastHj2VeWtlIqjjgW86_xjspAwoo8qqOptaQ">Peter Damian</a> wrote in 1050: </p>

<blockquote>
<p>“From various reports we are aware of the perverse and wholly detestable practice of certain people, who at the death of the bishop break in like enemies and rob his house, like thieves make off with his belongings, set fire to the homes on his estate, and with fierce and savage barbarity cut down his grape vines and orchards.”</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Early Christian elections were initially open to entire congregations. Though these elections often gave the lion’s share of voting power to the wealthy and well-connected, there was the general understanding that everyone would play a role: “<a href="https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/7794/vox-populi?srsltid=AfmBOorA7TQf3uG1zOvuLx5rwZaLYwoAbP4ey080XdXrkEi08ytsgMi5">vox populi, vox Dei</a>,” or “the voice of the people is the voice of God.”</p>

<p>However, by the end of the 13th century, the papacy had successfully established its authority over both ordinary people and secular rulers. On religious matters, there would no longer be public input. Instead, beginning in 1274, <a href="https://theconversation.com/papal-elections-arent-always-as-dramatic-as-conclave-but-the-history-behind-the-process-is-242958">a conclave of cardinals</a> elected the pope. The pope, sometimes still under the influence of higher lords, then nominated abbots and bishops. </p>

<p>The voice of the people had largely vanished. Nevertheless, they made themselves heard.</p>

<p>An <a href="https://brill.com/display/title/14615?language=en&amp;srsltid=AfmBOoqUJiDIauUJaKFgastHj2VeWtlIqjjgW86_xjspAwoo8qqOptaQ">April 1314</a> papal election in Carpentras, a small city in southeastern France, turned so violent that it delayed the naming of a new pope for nearly two years. </p>

<p>Deadlocked over the candidates, the cardinals dragged out the election for so long that frustrated locals attacked the episcopal palace where the conclave was being held. Cardinals and their staff fled and delayed until August 1316, when, under the protection of the French king’s forces, they nominated <a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-XXII">Pope John XXII</a>.</p>

<p>Over 60 years later, in March 1378, <a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gregory-XI">Pope Gregory XI</a> died. Amid threats from a crowd demanding an Italian pope, the cardinals elected <a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Urban-VI">Urban VI</a>, an Italian, the following month. But over the ensuing months, the cardinals soured on Urban and declared their election invalid on the grounds that they had acted under duress. They elected a rival pope, <a href="https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/magazine/article/great-papal-schism">triggering the Great Western Schism</a>, during which two competing papal courts existed from 1378 to 1417.</p>

<p>Violence could also erupt for seemingly minor affronts. </p>

<p>In October 1367, Pope Urban V was in Viterbo, Italy. The pope and his court were French. The Viterbese took offense when papal court officials washed a little dog in their fountain of Piano di Scarano, which served as a source of drinking water. A confrontation followed, <a href="https://brill.com/display/title/14615?language=en&amp;srsltid=AfmBOoqUJiDIauUJaKFgastHj2VeWtlIqjjgW86_xjspAwoo8qqOptaQ">which escalated into a two-day uprising</a>. The fountain was destroyed, and the pope and his cardinals were forced to take refuge in the Rocca Albornoz, the papal fortress. </p>

<h2>Authority is a two-way street</h2>

<p>Ideologies have evolved and technologies have advanced, but the fundamental struggle over who wields power, how authority earns legitimacy, and how compliance is enforced remains strikingly familiar.</p>

<p>The levers that leaders pull – taxation, welfare, infrastructure projects, propaganda, law enforcement – are largely the same, too.</p>

<p>Yet medieval folks understood that authority was a two-way street. When those in power didn’t hold up their end of the bargain, they were quick to resist, demand accountability and challenge authority. </p>

<p>In this sparring over power and consent, we can see, as one of Monty Python’s peasants put it, “the violence inherent in the system.”</p>

When Arthur explains that he was their king because the Lady of the Lake gave him Excalibur, one of the peasants objects: “Supreme executive power derives from a mandate from the masses, not from some farcical aquatic ceremony!” It also subverts the assumption that medieval people were politically passive, with resistance to abuses of authority largely absent before the Renaissance and the Protestant Reformation

Even if they didn’t speak in the language of Karl Marx, ordinary people back then held strong views about the working of political authority
And when they believed authorities had violated their obligations or lost their legitimacy, they routinely challenged rulers, bishops, tax collectors and urban elites
Enough is enough In the 11th and 12th centuries, northern French peasants famously resisted carrying out the work or paying the money that they owed to the lords who controlled the land they farmed
But perhaps the most well-known insurrection is the English Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 , the subject of the new film “ The Uprising ,” starring Andrew Garfield
After the first wave of the Black Death in 1348 created a massive labor shortage in Europe, workers were better positioned to negotiate for higher wages and better conditions
Serfs – peasants bound to the land and subject to a lord’s authority – increasingly pushed back against oppressive feudal obligations
In 1351, England’s King Edward III decreed the Statute of Laborers , which froze wages, derailing any aspiration for social mobility among the peasant class
Resentment continued to build with recurring episodes of the plague
Then, in 1381, Edward’s grandson and successor – 12-year-old King Richard II – instituted a one-time tax of 12 pence to raise funds for England’s ongoing war with France
Because the tax was charged per person rather than according to wealth, it placed a particularly heavy burden on poorer families
The people had had enough: Crowds attacked tax collectors and eventually organized into a larger movement, burning houses, castles and the records that documented their obligations to their lords
They killed government officials before marching to London to confront the king
The king met the rebels and pledged to abolish the poll tax and serfdom, while lowering the rent of agricultural land
He later recanted those promises: His forces hunted down the rebels, quashing the uprising

Together, they gave ordinary townspeople networks through which they could organize around shared interests and grievances
Over in France, the Hundred Years’ War caused a breakdown in authority
People were increasingly being asked to pay taxes they couldn’t afford
Unpaid troops routinely raided the countryside, and the French military suffered a number of significant military defeats

title: Why the Trump administration’s bid to end diversity efforts at nonprofit schools is likely to get tied up in court

<title>Why the Trump administration’s bid to end diversity efforts at nonprofit schools is likely to get tied up in court</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758963/original/file-20260909-50-bf6w11.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C201%2C4951%2C3300&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Some 18,000 private schools could be affected by a proposed new rule if it goes into effect.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/locust-walk-with-students-in-fall-university-of-news-photo/2148041311?adppopup=true">Jumping Rocks/Universal Images Group via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The Trump administration wants to strip all nonprofit colleges, universities and private K-12 schools of their <a href="https://apnews.com/article/harvard-nonprofit-tax-exempt-status-how-can-it-be-revoked-096614ea5ec65ec7a6ac08efd0f1e94f">tax-exempt status</a> if any of their programs designed to help students uses race as a criterion for eligibility. </p>

<p>This change is included in a rule the Treasury Department and <a href="https://apnews.com/article/tax-exempt-status-colleges-schools-trump-f8556ba3d94099df3c8aaa06fc13105f">Internal Revenue Service proposed on Sept. 3, 2026</a>. The rule could take effect after May 31, 2027, following a two-month-long comment period – as long as it’s not blocked or delayed by the legal challenges likely to arise.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://www.umass.edu/public-policy/about/directory/elizabeth-schmidt">nonprofit law scholar</a> who <a href="https://press.georgetown.edu/Book/Rules-of-the-Road-for-Nonprofit-Leaders">helps nonprofit leaders understand the legal issues they face</a>, I believe this latest salvo in the Trump administration’s attempt to <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/ending-illegal-discrimination-and-restoring-merit-based-opportunity/">end racial preferences</a> stretches U.S. law so far that it will likely be tied up in court for years.</p>



<h2>What is the Trump administration aiming to do?</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/04/2026-18127/racial-nondiscrimination-in-private-schools">proposed rule states</a> that private schools aren’t eligible for tax-exempt status if they have any school-administered or -supported program that “discriminates on the basis of race, color, or national or ethnic origin … for any purpose.”</p>

<p>The regulations do not define the word “discriminate” in this context, but Treasury Secretary <a href="https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/treasury-irs-move-to-end-tax-exempt-status-for-discriminatory-practices-in-private-schools">Scott Bessent has made clear</a> that the Trump administration considers programs that <a href="https://apnews.com/article/tax-exempt-status-colleges-schools-trump-f8556ba3d94099df3c8aaa06fc13105f">have diversity goals</a> to be a form of discrimination.</p>

<p>Private K-12 schools, colleges, universities and professional and trade schools would be subject to this rule, including all academic and athletic programs as well as all scholarships and admissions policies having anything to do with efforts to increase diversity.</p>

<p>The proposed rule would not apply to religious schools that make admitting people who adhere to the school’s religion a priority. Nor would it apply to public universities, but I believe the language is broad enough to apply to <a href="https://www.ibexinsights.co/data/rankings/public-endowment-per-ugds/">the foundations that provide scholarships</a> to students at public universities.</p>

<p>At this point, many key details about the rule remain unclear. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758964/original/file-20260909-50-xi4cfv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A group of women in graduation robes with kente cloth accents and in some cases a ribbon that says 'Harvard' listen and smile." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758964/original/file-20260909-50-xi4cfv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758964/original/file-20260909-50-xi4cfv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758964/original/file-20260909-50-xi4cfv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758964/original/file-20260909-50-xi4cfv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758964/original/file-20260909-50-xi4cfv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758964/original/file-20260909-50-xi4cfv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758964/original/file-20260909-50-xi4cfv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A group of graduates takes part in the Black Commencement at Harvard University on May 23, 2017.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/graduates-listen-to-the-master-of-ceremony-as-they-take-news-photo/687741592?adppopup=true">Keith Bedford/The Boston Globe via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The IRS estimates that this rule would <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/04/2026-18127/racial-nondiscrimination-in-private-schools">affect 18,000 private schools attended by 750,000 students</a> at all levels of instruction. </p>

<p>All private schools that are nonprofits depend on this tax exemption, both to <a href="https://minnesotanonprofits.org/resources-tools/starting-a-nonprofit/benefits-and-disadvantages-of-obtaining-501c3-tax-exemption">save money on income and property tax bills</a> and to <a href="https://taxpolicycenter.org/briefing-book/who-benefits-deduction-charitable-contributions">attract donations</a>. Without these benefits in place, tuition bills at nonprofit schools could skyrocket and the <a href="https://hechingerreport.org/pace-of-college-closings-picks-up-with-more-projected/">financial pressures many colleges and universities already face</a> would increase.</p>

<p>Americans <a href="https://theconversation.com/us-giving-grew-3-in-2025-crossing-the-600b-mark-for-the-first-time-282953">gave about US$92 billion in charitable donations</a> to private schools in 2025, which mostly supported higher education. That funding covers an average of about <a href="https://www.highereddive.com/news/college-donors-gifts-endowments-higher-ed-disruption-case-report/817378/">10% of college and university budgets</a>.</p>

<p>A change in the rules could also complicate schools’ relationships with their donors, alter the distribution of scholarships and lead to significant legal bills, as the <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/04/2026-18127/racial-nondiscrimination-in-private-schools">government itself has acknowledged</a>. </p>

<h2>What rationale has the administration provided?</h2>

<p>The proposed rule hinges on the Trump administration’s definition of racial discrimination: that any kind of <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2026/01/12/dei-civil-rights-trump-white-people/88147329007/">racial preference is wrong</a> and grounds for terminating government support – even when it’s meant to address past injustices, like the <a href="https://jimcrowmuseum.ferris.edu/timeline/jimcrow.htm">decades of systemic discrimination</a> that followed the end of slavery in the United States. </p>

<p>The IRS’ <a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/04/2026-18127/racial-nondiscrimination-in-private-schools">explanation of this rule</a> alludes to many legal precedents, including two significant U.S. Supreme Court decisions.</p>

<p>With its <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/461/574/">Bob Jones University v. United States</a> ruling, the court found in 1983 that a university banning interracial dating and marriage provided the IRS with the legal grounds to <a href="https://theconversation.com/can-trump-strip-harvard-of-its-charitable-status-scholars-of-nonprofit-law-and-accounting-describe-the-obstacles-in-his-way-255072">revoke its tax-exempt status</a>. </p>

<p>And the court found in 2023, in its <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/22pdf/20-1199_hgdj.pdf">Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard</a> ruling, that colleges and universities that accept government funding cannot consider race in their admissions policies without <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-2003-supreme-court-decision-upholding-affirmative-action-planted-the-seeds-of-its-overturning-as-justices-then-and-now-thought-racism-an-easily-solved-problem-208807">violating the equal protection clause</a> of the Constitution.</p>

<h2>Does the federal government have this authority?</h2>

<p>There is evidence that the government lacks the authority to implement this proposed rule. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.edweek.org/leadership/trump-extends-anti-dei-push-to-private-schools-eyeing-their-tax-exempt-status/2026/09">Educational groups, such as EdTrust</a> and the <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/09/04/nx-s1-5955666/irs-targets-private-schools-that-help-racial-minority-students">American Association of University Professors</a>, have expressed their opposition to the proposed changes. Legal scholars, such as <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/03/business/economy/trump-irs-college-nonprofits.html">Philip Hackney, Ellen Aprill, Daryll Jones</a> and <a href="https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2026-09-03/trump-tax-exempt-status-schools-race">Brian Galle</a>, have explained why the rule is likely illegal.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.studentloanplanner.com/pslf-rules-struck-down/">Two courts found</a> on June 30, 2026, that the Department of Education did not have the authority to alter <a href="https://theconversation.com/judges-block-trump-administrations-attempts-to-deny-access-to-public-service-loan-forgiveness-to-its-perceived-foes-286741">student loan forgiveness rules for the employees of nonprofits</a>. I expect to see opponents of the proposed rule to use those cases to support this argument. </p>

<p>Even if the courts determine the IRS does have authority to issue this rule, they <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/23pdf/22-451_7m58.pdf">will have the final say</a> as to whether the agency has interpreted congressional intent correctly. </p>

<p>Legal scholars are also saying that the Trump administration’s <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7193878">interpretation of prior Supreme Court cases</a> regarding discrimination at schools with tax-exempt status is incorrect. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.americanbar.org/groups/taxation/resources/tax-lawyer/2026-winter/revocation-tax-exemption-public-policy-illegality-terrorism-charitable-purpose/">They point out</a> that the Harvard admissions case was limited to colleges and universities that accepted public funding, and it provided some narrow exceptions. The proposed regulation would apply to all private schools, without exception, even if they don’t receive federal funding.</p>

<p>Further, the Bob Jones ruling stressed that a nonprofit’s tax-exempt status could only be revoked on “fundamental public policy” grounds when the activity in question so shocked the community conscience that it undermined any other benefit the institution conferred. It based its opinion on 30 years of evidence from all three branches of government to show that this kind of prejudice violated fundamental public policy.</p>

<p>The Trump administration <a href="https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7193878">may be unable to show</a> that the public’s perspective regarding diversity, equity and inclusion has changed that much. It <a href="https://www.justsecurity.org/107087/tracker-litigation-legal-challenges-trump-administration/">faces numerous lawsuits</a> challenging its definition of racial discrimination, and the American public <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-76761-8">remains overwhelmingly in favor</a> of diversity, equity and inclusion policies.</p>

<p>Law professor Roger Colinvaux has also <a href="https://www.philanthropy.com/opinion/what-the-fearless-fund-settlement-means-for-philanthropic-freedom/">pointed out</a> that interpreting the term “discrimination” to mean that organizations can no longer remedy past discrimination runs counter to the legal definition of the term “charitable,” which means to help those in need. <a href="https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-1/subject-group-ECFR062882ac6495890/section-1.501(c)(3)-1">Treasury Department regulations</a> define charitable activities as helping “the poor and disadvantaged” and eliminating “prejudice and discrimination.”</p>

<p>Finally, as Alexander Reid, a prominent attorney who specializes in tax exemptions, <a href="https://nonprofitlawblog.com/alex-reids-public-comments-fundamental-public-policy-regulations-on-racial-discrimination-in-schools/">noted in a letter to the IRS</a>, the proposed rule raises significant <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-1/">First Amendment issues of freedom of speech</a>, religion, association and institutional autonomy. That’s because it would affect choices that all private schools make that are essential to their identities and expression of ideas.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What’s at stake?</h2>

<p>Two years ago, the federal government <a href="https://www.eeoc.gov/newsroom/eeoc-delivers-administration-priorities-and-president-trumps-executive-orders">supported a definition</a> of racial discrimination that is <a href="https://civilrights.org/trump-rollbacks/">vastly different from the definition</a> the Trump administration now holds, and a new administration could come up with still another meaning. The lawsuits that will surely challenge this proposed rule will help to determine the legal meaning of racial discrimination – and Congress could weigh in as well.</p>

<p>In the meantime, many nonprofit schools may end their programs that are designed to address the results of past discrimination out of a fear of potentially losing their tax-exempt status.</p>

<p>I would not be surprised to see other kinds of nonprofits taking similar precautions as well, on the assumption that the Trump administration will apply this logic more broadly in the future.</p>

<p>The IRS will need to respond to the major themes addressed in the <a href="https://www.regulations.gov/document/IRS-2026-1189-0001">comments it receives</a> by Nov. 3, 2026. It may change the rule before it issues a final version.</p>

<p>And even if the rule were to be finalized on schedule, I would expect extensive litigation could delay or prevent its implementation.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291338/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>What the settlement left out: Meta can still collect data from kids</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759215/original/file-20260910-50-ahgznu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3129%2C2086&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Meta&#39;s surveillance business model has kids as well as adults in its sights.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/SocialMediaTrials/b5ea5e6282bf463fb68f05e946c6a14b/photo">AP Photo/Noah Berger</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In August 2026, Meta agreed to one of the largest <a href="https://coag.gov/app/uploads/2026/08/01-Exhibit-1-MDL-Consent-Judgment-FINAL-Settlment-Agreement-Fully-Executed.pdf">consumer protection settlements</a> in American history. The settlement resolves claims from 47 states alleging that Meta intentionally designed its Facebook and Instagram platforms to be addictive to young users and harmful to youth mental health. </p>

<p>As part of the settlement, Meta agreed to pay up to US$17.1 billion – approximately <a href="https://investor.atmeta.com/investor-news/press-release-details/2026/Meta-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Results/default.aspx">20% of Meta’s 2025 pretax profits</a> – in penalties over the next 10 years. Meta also agreed to <a href="https://theconversation.com/changes-to-facebook-and-instagram-are-key-part-of-metas-17b-settlement-with-the-states-over-harm-to-teens-290582">implement changes</a> to its platforms for young users, including daily time limits, access restrictions during school hours and late nights, and “productivity breaks” that interrupt scrolling every 60 minutes.</p>

<p>The $17.1 billion penalty and promised changes to the platforms have grabbed the headlines. But, as a law professor who <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=2KYB0PAAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">studies social media regulation</a>, I believe that what the settlement does not include will prove more important to youth safety in the long run. The settlement does not restrict Meta from continuing to collect data from young users, from using that data to sell its targeted ads, or from serving those targeted ads to young users. </p>

<p>In short, while Meta agreed to some limited changes to safeguard young users, it also succeeded in protecting its surveillance-based business model.</p>

<h2>How Meta makes money</h2>

<p>Meta’s core business is advertising. It is the world’s <a href="https://www.wsj.com/business/media/meta-expected-to-unseat-google-as-worlds-largest-digital-ad-player-83d3f522">second-largest digital advertising company</a> by revenue and will soon overtake Google to claim first place. Last year, Meta generated over <a href="https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1326801/000162828026003942/meta-20251231.htm#icc066a9e83ae4c46b57ee4d9dc9d7021_49">$200 billion in revenue</a>, up 22% over the prior year. </p>

<p>Meta’s growing revenue comes from delivering more ads to platform users and charging advertisers more for those ads. For Meta, maximizing the amount of time that users spend on its platforms is critical to revenue growth. The more time users spend on Meta’s platforms, the more ads Meta can serve to those users and, consequently, the more money Meta makes.</p>

<p>Meta’s ad business operates on a <a href="https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2019/03/harvard-professor-says-surveillance-capitalism-is-undermining-democracy/">surveillance model</a> that gives advertisers the ability to serve personalized ads to the users who are most likely to purchase the advertiser’s goods or services. Meta does this by collecting a <a href="https://www.facebook.com/privacy/policy/">large amount of data about platform users</a>. This data includes users’ friends, followers and other connections; the websites they visit, the apps they use, the games they play and the purchases they make; their demographics, including education level; the ads they see and how they interact with them; and how they use third parties’ products and services, online or in person.</p>

<p>The more time a user spends on Meta’s platforms, the more Meta learns about that user and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s43546-023-00501-9">the more effective its targeted ads</a> become. This means Meta has a strong incentive to keep users scrolling on its platforms and to collect as much data as possible from those users. The recent settlement does not change that incentive structure.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/fwNYjshqZ10?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Meta’s business model is an example of surveillance capitalism.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A history of breached settlements</h2>

<p>This is not the first time that Meta has settled with the government and agreed to change its platforms to improve user safety. In 2012, <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2012/08/ftc-approves-final-settlement-facebook">Meta, then Facebook, Inc., settled</a> with the Federal Trade Commission to resolve claims that it deceptively designed its privacy settings and collected data from users without their knowledge. </p>

<p>Then, in 2019, the FTC again sued Facebook, alleging that it violated the terms of the 2012 agreement by continuing to collect user data without consent. Again, <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2019/07/ftc-imposes-5-billion-penalty-sweeping-new-privacy-restrictions-facebook">the company settled</a>, agreeing to pay a $5 billion penalty and again promising to stop its deceptive data collection practices.</p>

<p>Based on Meta’s prior conduct violating the terms of its settlements, many observers <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2019/07/25/why-facebooks-billion-settlement-with-ftc-wont-change-thing/">questioned whether the $5 billion penalty</a> would deter Meta from continuing its data collection practices. It did not take long to get an answer. </p>

<p>In 2023, the FTC brought yet another action against Meta, alleging that it had violated the terms of the 2019 settlement. As a result of this violation, the FTC <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2023/05/ftc-proposes-blanket-prohibition-preventing-facebook-monetizing-youth-data">sought to restrict</a> Meta from collecting and monetizing the data of young users. </p>

<p>Meta responded by challenging the FTC’s authority to impose those restrictions. Litigation in that case is ongoing.</p>

<h2>Meta’s incentives remain the same</h2>

<p>In 2026, Meta has again settled with the government, again paid a penalty and again promised changes. And again, those promises do not restrict it from collecting data and monetizing young users, nor does the settlement restrict Meta from continuing to serve young users targeted ads. </p>

<p>Youth safety advocates and legislators have long fought to <a href="https://rollcall.com/2026/09/01/panel-punts-kids-social-media-ban-for-data-consent-mandate/">stop social media platforms</a> from collecting data from young users and targeting ads to them. They have argued that doing so would remove social media companies’ incentive to design platforms that addict young people. By not including data collection and targeting restrictions in the settlement, I believe that the states missed an opportunity to change this incentive structure.</p>

<p>Repeatedly violating the terms of its settlements with the government seems to be an effective strategy for Meta. The company has learned that penalties for doing so are small in comparison with the profits gained through its conduct. This recent settlement looks like more of the same. With this pattern in mind, it is fair to ask whether the settlement will provide meaningful protection for young social media users or just allow Meta to continue with business as usual.</p>

<p>As former FTC Commissioner Rohit Chopra <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/documents/public_statements/1536911/chopra_dissenting_statement_on_facebook_7-24-19.pdf">stated when dissenting</a> from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, “When companies can violate the law, pay big penalties and still turn a profit while keeping their business model intact, enforcement agencies cannot claim victory.” </p>

<p>I believe this most recent settlement repeats the patterns of the past and continues to leave young users vulnerable on Meta’s platforms.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291130/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

And again, those promises do not restrict it from collecting data and monetizing young users, nor does the settlement restrict Meta from continuing to serve young users targeted ads
Youth safety advocates and legislators have long fought to stop social media platforms from collecting data from young users and targeting ads to them
They have argued that doing so would remove social media companies’ incentive to design platforms that addict young people
By not including data collection and targeting restrictions in the settlement, I believe that the states missed an opportunity to change this incentive structure
Repeatedly violating the terms of its settlements with the government seems to be an effective strategy for Meta
The company has learned that penalties for doing so are small in comparison with the profits gained through its conduct
This recent settlement looks like more of the same
With this pattern in mind, it is fair to ask whether the settlement will provide meaningful protection for young social media users or just allow Meta to continue with business as usual

As former FTC Commissioner Rohit Chopra stated when dissenting from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, “When companies can violate the law, pay big penalties and still turn a profit while keeping their business model intact, enforcement agencies cannot claim victory.” I believe this most recent settlement repeats the patterns of the past and continues to leave young users vulnerable on Meta’s platforms

title: 25 years after 9/11, the GOP has never been more anti-Muslim

body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rudy Giuliani arrive ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum in Manhattan on September 11, 2026. | Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Hi readers — today marks 25 years since 9/11
In New York City, Washington, and Pennsylvania, survivors, families, and politicians are gathering to grieve and commemorate the attacks

Today, we wanted to focus on one small part of the story in New York City, where former Mayor Rudy Giuliani singled out Mayor Zohran Mamdani , who is Muslim, with an Islamophobic screed about Mamdani’s participation in memorial ceremonies

Giuliani’s rant, to be clear, is not really news in its own right; 25 years on, he’s less “America’s mayor” than he is the twice – disbarred , disgraced former lawyer of President Donald Trump. (And Mamdani did attend the event, even shaking hands with Giuliani.) But Giuliani’s remarks are, unfortunately, emblematic of a disturbing trend in Republican politics, where open, aggressive Islamophobia is on the rise — 25 years after a particularly ugly brand of it emerged in response to 9/11
One major difference between then and now? In 2001, many politicians tried to tamp it down rather than inflame it

As Nathan Lean, an assistant teaching professor at North Carolina State University and author of the book The Islamophobia Industry , explained to my colleague Christian Paz last month : “Islamophobia has passed the dinner table test
You can say things about Muslims with basic impunity today

And it’s institutionalized in the way that prejudice that targets other marginalized communities is not.” The GOP is running on Islamophobia in 2026 The 2026 midterm elections have provided a particularly clear showcase for the right’s Islamophobic turn.  On Thursday, at the second and final night of the GOP’s unusual midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, Sen
Ted Cruz (R-TX) told attendees that “communism” and “Islamism” were allying against Republicans. “They share the same enemies,” he said. “They hate Christians

They hate the Constitution, and they hate America.”  At another point in Cruz’s speech, attendees screamed “he should be shot” as Cruz name-checked Mamdani, Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (who is Muslim, and who Cruz said “says he has an obligation to Sharia Law”), and Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.  As Christian reports , Michigan and especially Texas have both been on the front lines of rising Islamophobia.  Michigan has a large Muslim population in cities like Dearborn and Hamtramck, and El-Sayed has drawn particular vitriol; Rep

Nancy Mace (R-SC) wrote last month that “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic.”  And in Texas, as the New York Times reported at length last month , Islamophobia has become a matter of policy as well as rhetoric from Republican Gov

Greg Abbott and other politicians in the state.  El-Sayed, in Michigan, has described the attacks as an attempt to distract voters from other issues. “They’re going to point at me, they’re going to point at my name, like, ‘Wow, he’s different,’” he said last month . “My name is not raising your gas prices
My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.” Without much else to run on , though, Republicans seem to have decided they’re all-in on Islamophobia

On Vox’s Unexplainable podcast, the Switched on Pop team looks at how our brains can figure out a song just from its first few seconds, how it can influence our perception, and what we’re losing as recent hits begin to move away from intros.  Before you go… Did you know… that young readers tend to drop off around age 9 , even if they’re prolific readers before that? Publishers aren’t exactly sure why — but they’re hoping a new approach to “middle-grade books” could help reverse some of the decline.  Today’s trivia: Which country voted against restarting membership talks with the European Union this year? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword

title: The one thing you can do to help a whole lot of animals, explained in 4 charts
excerpt: Many people, when they learn about the horrors of factory farming , become vegetarian or vegan
body: Many people, when they learn about the horrors of factory farming , become vegetarian or vegan
I’m one of those people, and it stuck — I haven’t eaten meat in 20 years
But new research highlights how ditching meat isn’t the only option to help animals on factory farms

There’s actually one thing that’s almost as effective and probably way easier for most people: eating fewer small animals.  The number of animals who suffer to produce food products — and how much they suffer — varies widely
Bigger animals, like cattle raised for beef, are raised in lower numbers and aren’t treated as terribly as smaller animals, like farmed fish and chickens
And because fish and chickens are so small, far more of them must be farmed to produce the same amount of meat as large animals

A family sitting down for a steak dinner, for example, will probably consume about half a percent of one cow, while a family eating a rotisserie chicken might eat the whole bird.  Animal advocates call it the “small body problem,” and it’s the subject of a new analysis published by Chris Bryant , an honorary research associate at the University of Bath in the UK, and Faunalytics , an animal welfare research group

The researchers wanted to answer a simple but consequential question: How much animal suffering is embedded in each bite of meat we eat or egg we consume?  “We are somewhat used to seeing, especially from the climate movement, data and other kinds of tools that help us think about the carbon footprint of the choices that we make, and we think that’s really important,” Allison Troy, Faunalytics’ research director, told me. “But we felt like there was a gap in terms of thinking about more of a ‘suffering footprint’ when it comes to choosing to purchase animal products.” This gives us a new way to think about how we eat, and how it affects the animals trapped in factory farms

If you don’t want to go fully plant-based, what about cutting back — specifically — on meat from small animals? Unpacking the small body problem To quantify the “suffering footprint” of everyday animal products consumers eat, the researchers analyzed data from the US Department of Agriculture, the United Nations, and other sources to determine how much edible meat — or eggs or milk — each type of farmed animal produces throughout a typical lifespan on a farm
They also incorporated indirect sources of animal suffering in their calculations
For example, some farmed fish species are fed other fish, and these “feeder” fish were factored into the data

Then the researchers crunched the numbers to figure out two things: how many days of animal suffering are embedded in a pound of various animal products, and how many animal lives are slaughtered per pound for those products
The analysis found that the vast majority of animal suffering from our diets comes from one tiny animal: shrimp
That means that a single bite of your shrimp scampi is far more harmful than devouring an entire burger
But seafood doesn’t account for a large portion of most Americans’ diets , and many of us eat none at all
When seafood is removed from the data, cutting back on poultry products — chicken meat, turkey meat, and eggs — is the most effective way to limit the amount of suffering caused by one’s diet

This enormous disparity in poultry versus other categories “is driven by the fact that those are smaller-bodied animals — it just takes a larger number of animals to produce consumable products for people,” Troy said. “And I don’t think that that’s often a way that people think about animal products when they’re making these decisions.”  Chickens and turkeys also tend to be treated worse than cattle and pigs

Chickens raised for meat, for example, have been bred to grow so fast , and so big, that many have difficulty standing and walking, while half of hens raised for eggs in the US are confined in small cages for their entire lives.  That doesn’t mean pigs and cattle have it easy — far from it
Pork producers, for example, typically castrate and teeth-clip piglets without pain relief, and the pigs spend their lives indoors
Female breeding pigs , like caged hens, are confined in tiny cages
And beef cattle are branded and dehorned , often without pain relief, and spend their final months in feedlots

But because these animals are so much bigger, each produces a lot more meat than smaller animals.  In other words, their suffering is spread out across many more bites of bacon or burgers.  Going beyond the numbers The report wasn’t peer-reviewed, and I reached out to Trevor Woolley — an assistant professor of agricultural and applied economics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison — for his thoughts

Woolley told me over email that it’s “important to recognize that the numbers that are included in their equation are estimates,” and that “the exact numbers should not be taken as precise, but in the right ballpark.” How should I think about eggs?  It might come as a surprise that eating fewer eggs is one of the best actions you can take to help animals, considering it doesn’t require killing animals

Still, egg-laying hens tend to have poor welfare; about half of them in the US are in tiny cages where they can’t flap their wings for their entire lives, and the tips of their beaks are seared off without pain relief
Once their productivity wanes — at about 1.5 years of age — they’re slaughtered for meat

Eating fewer eggs , and getting “pasture-raised” eggs when you do buy them, can help (if you’re looking for information on what the various buzzwords on egg cartons actually mean, we’ve got you covered ). “Comparing animal products in terms of lives and (especially) days broadly makes sense,” Woolley added. “‘Days’ is a really nice metric because farm animal species have such drastically different lifespans on the farm.” There is, however, one major limitation to the research: it doesn’t factor in the severity of suffering that different animals experience. “We made a choice methodologically to define ‘animal suffering’ as days of life [on a farm],” Troy said. “And I think that that’s a useful, albeit simple, metric
But it is not the only one.” For example, on a day-to-day basis, dairy cows don’t seem to have it as bad as an egg-laying hen in a cage
But dairy cows tend to be farmed for twice as many years as hens

Does that suffering over many years compound in a way that, if we could fully understand it, would change the calculation? This analysis can’t answer nuanced questions like that, though other animal welfare researchers are working to provide a more comprehensive picture. “If you can stand to think about it long enough, the problem becomes paralyzing,” my colleague Marina Bolotnikova has written about factory farming. “Tens of billions of land animals are slaughtered every year; hundreds of millions every day; thousands in the time it takes to read this sentence
The number grows by billions more every year, into multiples that feel as abysmal as they are mind-numbing.” It’s enough to cause a lot of people to tune out and ignore the problem altogether
But shrinking these figures down to the impact our own diets have on animals is much more manageable
We can think smaller and maybe, while we’re at it, eat fewer small animals.

title: Trump keeps telling voters he doesn’t care much about affordability
excerpt: President Donald Trump during the first day of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on September 9, 2026. | Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images If the mi
body: President Donald Trump during the first day of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on September 9, 2026. | Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images If the midterms were a referendum on whether trans athletes should be barred from women’s sports, or the White House ballroom should be gorgeously renovated , or God should be identified as “nonbinary,” then Republicans would have a clear and confident closing message
Key takeaways The cost of living is midterm voters’ top issue
The war in Iran has led to the first decline in real wages since 2023
Trump could bring gas prices down before Election Day by seeking a ceasefire with Iran, but he’s choosing to prioritize military victory
The president is also escalating trade wars, despite their impact on consumer prices
Unfortunately for the GOP, voters are less concerned with the Christian deity’s preferred pronouns than with their own cost of living

Which is understandable: Diesel fuel prices just hit a record high, mortgage rates are climbing , and groceries keep getting more expensive.  Due partly to these trends, Republicans are poorly positioned to win an argument about inflation — and are only growing more so, as Election Day nears
This was apparent before President Donald Trump convened the first-ever Republican midterm convention in Dallas this week
But the festivities underscored the GOP’s predicament and the many ways that Trump is personally exacerbating it
Many Republican speakers did address the subject of affordability in Dallas
And the party’s broad narrative is straightforward enough: Democrats created the cost-of-living crisis, Republicans alleviated it by cutting your taxes
Americans might still disdain President Joe Biden’s economic management
Yet they’re far more likely to blame high prices on the current president than the previous one, according to polls.  And not without reason
After all, it was Trump — not Biden — who engineered an oil shock and global trade war
Tellingly, on Wednesday night, all four battleground state Senate candidates — Ken Paxton, Jon Husted, Michael Whatley, and Mike Collins — made no mention of the Iran war or of Trump’s tariffs
If Republican frontliners are clear-eyed about their party’s liabilities, Trump seems largely indifferent to them
Historically, presidents have often made an effort to limit election-year price increases — and/or, to reduce the salience of their party’s worst issues
Yet Trump has been doing the very opposite.  In recent weeks, the president has escalated his conflict with Iran and his trade war with US allies , driving up Americans’ costs in the process
And he’s been remarkably frank about his refusal to prioritize affordability
In his remarks to the convention Wednesday, Trump impersonated a disaffected constituent, saying, “You know, I wish you didn’t do the war in Iran

Gasoline’s up, ba ba ba” — before explaining to this critic that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon took precedence over their energy costs.  Republicans may still weather a midterm backlash
The party remains narrowly favored to retain the Senate, while gerrymandered maps should limit its losses in the House
But if this year’s “blue wave” proves less than tidal, it will be in spite of Trump’s efforts, not because of them

The GOP’s very simple problem The Republican Party’s fundamental problem is simple: Voters’ top concern is the cost of living — and American purchasing power has fallen sharply in 2026, as a direct result of the president’s policies
In virtually every poll, a plurality of voters name “ inflation ,” “ the cost of living ,” or “ affordability ” as their most important issue
And they are not impressed with Trump’s record on that front

In a recent Ipsos survey, 74 percent of respondents said that their cost of living is “off on the wrong track.” Meanwhile, in Nate Silver’s poll tracker , more than 70 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of inflation, up from just 41 percent when he took office
Silver Bulletin " /> During his first year in office, Trump could have reasonably argued that voters were giving him a bad rap on the economy
After all, real wages — how much Americans earn per hour, adjusted for inflation — actually rose in 2025, even as disapproval of the president’s economic record surged

But in February 2026, Trump brought nearly three years of real wage growth to a screeching halt: By launching a war with Iran — and thus, triggering its closure of the Strait of Hormuz — Trump triggered the first sustained decline in Americans’ purchasing power since 2022

View Link According to an estimate from Brown’s Watson School, the Iran war has cost the average US household more than $780 through elevated energy prices.  Politically, this seems to have made a real difference
At the beginning of March, Trump’s net approval rating on inflation was -28, according to Nate Silver’s polling average; as of this writing, it is -45.9
At this point, there may be little Trump can do to gain broad public trust on the cost of living
But political science research suggests that economic trends in the runup to Election Day can shift votes at the margin
And precisely because this year’s price spike is largely self-inflicted, Trump has an unusual amount of power to increase affordability before Americans head to the polls
All he’d need to do is reach a ceasefire (or, ideally, peace deal) with Iran
We know Trump could bring down energy costs by pursuing peace because he already has

Throughout 2026, oil prices have consistently fallen whenever the US-Iran war has cooled off  — and risen whenever it has intensified.  When Trump signaled an imminent ceasefire deal in early June , the price of an oil barrel swiftly fell, dropping below $75
Once that ceasefire broke down early the next month, oil prices resumed their climb, until Trump paused US strikes on July 25
